# WebAuthn ceremony timeout: Level 3 Recommendation vs Level 2 when userVerification is 'discouraged'

## Verdict (one line)

Level 3 gives a **single, unconditional** recommendation — **range 300000 ms to 600000 ms (5–10 minutes), default 300000 ms (5 minutes)** — in §15.1 "Recommended Range for Ceremony Timeouts". Level 2 instead **made the recommendation conditional on userVerification**: when it is `"discouraged"` the recommended range was **30000 ms to 180000 ms (30 s–3 min)** with a recommended default of **120000 ms (2 minutes)**, while for `"required"`/`"preferred"` it used 30000–600000 ms with a 300000 ms default. The discouraged case is therefore exactly where the two levels diverge: Level 2's discouraged ceiling (180000 ms) sits **120000 ms below** Level 3's floor (300000 ms).

## 1. Level 3 — the values asked for

Source: W3C *Web Authentication: An API for accessing Public Key Credentials Level 3*, W3C Recommendation, dated 25 August 2026 — `https://www.w3.org/TR/2026/REC-webauthn-3-20260825/`. The identical §15.1 text is served from `https://www.w3.org/TR/webauthn-3/Overview.html` (same document hash) and from `https://www.w3.org/TR/webauthn-4/`.

§15.1 states, in full:

> "Ceremonies relying on timing, e.g., a registration ceremony (see timeout) or an authentication ceremony (see timeout), ought to follow [WCAG21]'s Guideline 2.2 Enough Time. If a client platform determines that a Relying Party-supplied timeout does not appropriately adhere to the latter [WCAG21] guidelines, then the client platform MAY adjust the timeout accordingly.
>
> The recommended range and default for a WebAuthn ceremony timeout is as follows:
>
> **Recommended range: 300000 milliseconds to 600000 milliseconds.**
>
> **Recommended default value: 300000 milliseconds (5 minutes).**"

| Item | Milliseconds | Seconds / minutes |
|---|---|---|
| Recommended range, lower bound | 300000 ms | 300 s = 5 min |
| Recommended range, upper bound | 600000 ms | 600 s = 10 min |
| Recommended default value | 300000 ms | 300 s = 5 min |

Key structural point: §15.1 contains **no `userVerification` branch**. The same range and default are recommended for every ceremony, whether user verification is `required`, `preferred`, or `discouraged`.

## 2. Level 2 — the values it used, and where they lived

Source: *Web Authentication: An API for accessing Public Key Credentials Level 2*, W3C Recommendation — `https://www.w3.org/TR/webauthn-2/`. (The same conditional tables appear in the Level 2 Candidate Recommendation-era Working Draft `https://www.w3.org/TR/2019/WD-webauthn-2-20191126/`, so this is not a late editorial change.)

Level 2 put the recommendation **inside the ceremony algorithms**, in two places, and both were conditional:

**a) Registration — `navigator.credentials.create()`, keyed on `options.authenticatorSelection.userVerification`:**

> "If the timeout member of options is present, check if its value lies within a reasonable range as defined by the client and if not, correct it to the closest value lying within that range. Set a timer lifetimeTimer to this adjusted value. If the timeout member of options is not present, then set lifetimeTimer to a client-specific default.
>
> Recommended ranges and defaults for the timeout member of options are as follows.
>
> If options.authenticatorSelection.userVerification is set to **discouraged** — Recommended range: **30000 milliseconds to 180000 milliseconds.** Recommended default value: **120000 milliseconds (2 minutes).**
>
> is set to **required or preferred** — Recommended range: **30000 milliseconds to 600000 milliseconds.** Recommended default value: **300000 milliseconds (5 minutes).**
>
> Note: The user agent should take cognitive guidelines into considerations regarding timeout for users with special needs."

**b) Authentication — `navigator.credentials.get()`, keyed on `options.userVerification`:** the same two-row table, identical numbers, with the condition expressed on `options.userVerification` instead of `options.authenticatorSelection.userVerification`.

| Level 2 condition | Recommended range | Recommended default |
|---|---|---|
| `userVerification` = `"discouraged"` | 30000 ms – 180000 ms (30 s – 3 min) | 120000 ms (2 min) |
| `userVerification` = `"required"` or `"preferred"` | 30000 ms – 600000 ms (30 s – 10 min) | 300000 ms (5 min) |

## 3. How Level 2 differed — the difference stated precisely

The divergence is not a single number; it is four distinct changes. For a relying party or client porting behaviour, all four matter.

1. **Conditional vs. unconditional.** Level 2 gave *two* recommendations selected by `userVerification`; Level 3 gives *one* recommendation for all ceremonies. In Level 3 there is no longer any spec-sanctioned reason to shorten a timeout because user verification is discouraged.
2. **The discouraged case changed in both bounds and in the default.** L2 discouraged: 30000–180000 ms, default 120000 ms. L3 (all cases): 300000–600000 ms, default 300000 ms. The default rises by **180000 ms** (2 min → 5 min); the lower bound rises by **270000 ms** (30000 → 300000); the upper bound rises by **420000 ms** (180000 → 600000). The L2 discouraged range and the L3 range are **disjoint**: 180000 ms < 300000 ms, a gap of **120000 ms**.
3. **The required/preferred case also moved at the floor.** L2 required/preferred was 30000–600000 ms with a 300000 ms default; L3 is 300000–600000 ms with a 300000 ms default. Same default and same ceiling, but the floor rises from 30000 ms to 300000 ms — i.e. a 30-second timeout, acceptable under L2 for any userVerification value, is below the Level 3 recommended range.
4. **Location and framing.** Level 2 embedded the table in the create() and get() algorithm steps. Level 3 lifts it to a dedicated §15.1, immediately preceding §16 Test Vectors, and frames it by reference to WCAG 2.1 Guideline 2.2 "Enough Time" and to the client platform's permission to adjust an RP-supplied timeout that does not appropriately adhere to those guidelines.

A one-row comparison of the case the question names:

| | userVerification = `"discouraged"` |
|---|---|
| **Level 2 Recommendation** | range **30000–180000 ms**; default **120000 ms** (2 min) |
| **Level 3 Recommendation** | range **300000–600000 ms**; default **300000 ms** (5 min) — not varied by userVerification |

## 4. Normative weight (do not over-read these numbers as MUSTs)

- §15.1 of Level 3 is written as guidance: ceremonies "**ought to**" follow WCAG 2.1 Guideline 2.2, and a client platform "**MAY** adjust" a non-conforming RP-supplied timeout. There is no MUST in §15.1 requiring a relying party to submit a value in 300000–600000 ms.
- What *is* normative is the algorithm behaviour, present in both levels: if `timeout` is present, the client checks whether it "lies within a reasonable range as defined by the client" and, if not, "correct[s] it to the closest value lying within that range"; if `timeout` is absent, the client uses "a client-specific default". The published recommendations are the guidance for choosing those client-side bounds and default, not an override of client discretion.
- Level 2 likewise used "Recommended ranges and defaults", not MUST language, for the same table, plus the informative note that "the user agent should take cognitive guidelines into considerations regarding timeout for users with special needs" (a note Level 3 replaces with the WCAG 2.1 reference).

## 5. Consistency check performed on the figures above

- Unit conversions: 30000 ms = 30 s; 180000 ms = 180 s = 3 min; 120000 ms = 120 s = 2 min; 300000 ms = 300 s = 5 min (matches the spec's own "(5 minutes)"); 600000 ms = 600 s = 10 min. No conversion contradicts a parenthetical in the quoted text.
- Ordering: every stated range satisfies lower < default ≤ upper — L2 discouraged 30000 < 120000 ≤ 180000; L2 required/preferred 30000 < 300000 ≤ 600000; L3 300000 ≤ 300000 ≤ 600000.
- Cross-level: the claim "L3's floor exceeds L2's discouraged ceiling" holds numerically (300000 > 180000) and is stated as a 120000 ms gap; the claim "L2 required/preferred ceiling equals L3 ceiling" holds (600000 = 600000). The two levels' ranges are never described as nested.

## 6. What an implementer should do with this

- **Relying party:** supply `timeout` in **300000–600000 ms**; if you have no reason to pick otherwise, use **300000 ms** (the Level 3 recommended default). Do not carry forward a Level 2-era 120000 ms timeout chosen because `userVerification: "discouraged"` — under Level 3 that value is below the recommended range, and a conforming client is entitled to clamp it upward to its own floor.
- **Client platform:** pick the "reasonable range" and the "client-specific default" to match §15.1 (300000–600000 ms, default 300000 ms), clamp out-of-range RP values to the nearest bound, and apply the WCAG 2.1 Guideline 2.2 adjustment latitude. If you must keep a shorter ceiling for a specific UX (e.g. a cross-device hybrid flow), document it as a deliberate deviation from §15.1, not as Level 2 behaviour.
- **Auditors / conformance reviews:** cite §15.1 of the Level 3 REC for the 300000/600000/300000 figures, and the create()/get() algorithm text of the Level 2 REC for the 30000/180000/120000 discouraged figures. Note that the Level 2 numbers were guidance inside an algorithm, so a Level 2 implementation that used a 5-minute timeout in the discouraged case was not non-conformant — it was outside the *recommendation*.

## 7. Scope and caveats

- Level 3 figures are pinned to the dated Recommendation **REC-webauthn-3-20260825**; the living `/TR/webauthn-3/Overview.html` and `/TR/webauthn-4/` served byte-identical §15.1 text at retrieval, so the answer is not sensitive to which of those three URLs is used, but it *is* pinned to that REC generation.
- Level 2 figures are from the published Level 2 Recommendation; the 2019 Level 2 Working Draft shows the same numbers, so no draft-vs-REC drift affects the comparison.
- The `userVerification` enumeration itself is unchanged across levels — `"required"`, `"preferred"`, `"discouraged"`, where `"discouraged"` means "the Relying Party does not want user verification employed during the operation (e.g., in the interest of minimizing disruption to the user interaction flow)". What changed is only whether the timeout recommendation keys off that value.
- This answer is limited to the timeout recommendation. It does not evaluate browser or authenticator implementations' actual clamping behaviour, and it makes no claim about how any specific client chooses its "reasonable range".

question: X28
answer:
ANSWER (RFC 9293, §3.7.1 'Maximum Segment Size Option')

If a TCP endpoint receives no MSS option at connection setup, it MUST assume a default send MSS of 536 octets for IPv4 (576 - 40) and 1220 octets for IPv6 (1280 - 60). The requirement level is MUST, carrying the requirement tag MUST-15 in RFC 9293's own requirement table.

  Address family | Default send MSS | Derivation        | Requirement
  ---------------+------------------+-------------------+----------------------
  IPv4           | 536 octets       | 576 - 40          | MUST (MUST-15)
  IPv6           | 1220 octets      | 1280 - 60         | MUST (MUST-15)

1. AUTHORITATIVE TEXT

RFC 9293, Section 3.7.1, verbatim:

  "TCP endpoints MUST implement both sending and receiving the MSS
   Option (MUST-14).

   TCP implementations SHOULD send an MSS Option in every SYN segment
   when its receive MSS differs from the default 536 for IPv4 or 1220
   for IPv6 (SHLD-5), and MAY send it always (MAY-3).

   If an MSS Option is not received at connection setup, TCP
   implementations MUST assume a default send MSS of 536 (576 - 40) for
   IPv4 or 1220 (1280 - 60) for IPv6 (MUST-15).

   The maximum size of a segment that a TCP endpoint really sends, the
   'effective send MSS', MUST be the smaller (MUST-16) of the send MSS
   (that reflects the available reassembly buffer size at the remote
   host, the EMTU_R [19]) and the largest transmission size permitted by
   the IP layer (EMTU_S [19]):

   Eff.snd.MSS = min(SendMSS+20, MMS_S) - TCPhdrsize - IPoptionsize

   where:

   *  SendMSS is the MSS value received from the remote host, or the
      default 536 for IPv4 or 1220 for IPv6, if no MSS Option is
      received.
   *  MMS_S is the maximum size for a transport-layer message that TCP
      may send."

Source: RFC 9293 (STD 7), W. Eddy, Ed., August 2022, DOI 10.17487/RFC9293, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.xml>, Section 3.7.1. The inline-errata rendering of the same document (<https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/inline-errata/rfc9293.html>) reproduces this paragraph with identical wording and identical values, so no erratum in force at retrieval alters 536, 1220, or MUST-15.

2. REQUIREMENT LEVEL — PRECISELY WHAT IS AND IS NOT MANDATED

The keyword is MUST in the RFC 2119 / RFC 8174 (BCP 14) sense, and RFC 9293 tags it MUST-15. This is confirmed twice inside RFC 9293 itself:

  (a) The prose sentence above uses the uppercase 'MUST assume'.
  (b) The requirements table in the RFC's implementation-status appendix lists, in the column for mandatory requirements:
        "IPv4 Send-MSS default is 536"   -> MUST-15
        "IPv6 Send-MSS default is 1220"  -> MUST-15

Do not conflate MUST-15 with the neighbouring MSS requirements, which have different levels:

  MUST-14  Implement both sending and receiving the MSS Option — MUST.
  SHLD-5   Send an MSS Option in every SYN when the receive MSS differs from the default (536 IPv4 / 1220 IPv6) — SHOULD.
  MAY-3    Send an MSS Option always — MAY.
  MUST-15  Assume the 536 / 1220 default send MSS when no MSS Option is received — MUST.  <-- the ask
  MUST-16  Effective send MSS = min(send MSS, IP-layer permitted size) — MUST.
  SHLD-6   MSS accounts for varying MTU — SHOULD.
  MUST-65  MSS not sent on non-SYN segments — MUST.
  MUST-67  MSS value based on MMS_R — MUST.

Note the asymmetry: sending the option is only a SHOULD (SHLD-5) or MAY (MAY-3), but assuming the default when the option is absent is a MUST (MUST-15). An implementation may therefore legally omit the MSS option and still be conformant, but it can never legally guess at a missing option's value — it must fall back to exactly 536 (IPv4) or 1220 (IPv6).

3. DERIVATION OF THE TWO NUMBERS

IPv4: 576 - 40 = 536.
  - 576 is the IPv4 default effective MTU for destinations not directly connected (RFC 1122 recommendation, incorporated by reference; RFC 9293 §3.7.2 discusses this value as the fixed default that PMTUD/PLPMTUD exist to improve upon).
  - 40 = 20-byte IPv4 header + 20-byte TCP header (no IP options assumed).
  - Check: 536 + 40 = 576 — the default send MSS plus headers exactly fills the assumed MTU; it does not exceed it.

IPv6: 1280 - 60 = 1220.
  - 1280 is the IPv6 minimum link MTU (RFC 8200).
  - 60 = 40-byte IPv6 fixed header + 20-byte TCP header.
  - Check: 1220 + 60 = 1280 — exact fit, no overflow.

Both figures are octets of TCP payload, i.e. the MSS counts only the data field of the segment and excludes the TCP header and all IP headers. This is why the subtrahends are header sizes and not segment sizes.

4. SCOPE AND OVERRIDE RULES AN IMPLEMENTER MUST APPLY

  - These are fallbacks, used only when no MSS option arrives at connection setup. If an MSS option is received, the received value is SendMSS and the defaults do not apply ("SendMSS is the MSS value received from the remote host, or the default 536 for IPv4 or 1220 for IPv6, if no MSS Option is received").
  - The MSS option appears only in SYN segments (MUST-65). Absence of the option in a non-SYN segment carries no information and must not trigger the fallback.
  - The 536 / 1220 values are a ceiling on what may be assumed, not a licence to send 536-octet segments regardless of path. The value actually transmitted is the effective send MSS, MUST-16:
        Eff.snd.MSS = min(SendMSS + 20, MMS_S) - TCPhdrsize - IPoptionsize
    which is the smaller of the send MSS and the largest size the IP layer permits (EMTU_S), minus TCP header and IP option sizes. With path MTU smaller than the assumed MTU, the effective send MSS is below 536 / 1220.
  - A local MSS option, if sent, must be derived from the receive-side reassembly limit (MMS_R, MUST-67), not from these defaults; the defaults describe what you assume about the peer, not what you advertise.
  - Do not confuse these with the send-window default. The 536 / 1220 figures are MSS (segment payload size); the default send window is a separate 16-bit field with its own 65535-octet ceiling. They are unrelated numbers and neither constrains the other.
  - Path MTU Discovery / PLPMTUD (RFC 9293 §3.7.2) is strongly recommended to improve on the fixed 576 / 1280 assumptions, but it does not change the MUST-15 fallback values at connection setup.
  - IPv6 does not carry a MUST to always emit an MSS option in RFC 9293; that behaviour is SHOULD-when-differing (SHLD-5) or MAY-always (MAY-3). Any claim of a mandatory IPv6 MSS-option emission is not supported by this text.

5. CONFORMANCE CHECKS (what a reviewer should test)

  C1. Peer SYN carries no MSS option over IPv4 -> implementation's SendMSS variable = 536. Pass/fail: exact equality, not 'approximately 576'.
  C2. Peer SYN carries no MSS option over IPv6 -> SendMSS = 1220.
  C3. Peer SYN carries MSS option with value X -> SendMSS = X; the defaults are not consulted.
  C4. Effective send MSS computed as min(SendMSS + 20, MMS_S) - TCPhdrsize - IPoptionsize and never exceeding the IP-layer permitted size (MUST-16).
  C5. Requirement traceability: 536 and 1220 map to MUST-15 in the implementation's requirement matrix; the matrix must not list them as SHOULD.

6. ONE-LINE ANSWER

Under RFC 9293 §3.7.1, an endpoint that receives no MSS option at connection setup MUST (MUST-15) assume a default send MSS of 536 octets for IPv4 and 1220 octets for IPv6.

question: X29
shape: Consumer-product RF safety: microwave oven leakage (Canada, Radiation Emitting Devices Regulations; US FDA 21 CFR 1030.10)
answer:
MICROWAVE-OVEN LEAKAGE POWER-DENSITY LIMITS — CANADA vs. US, AT >= 5 cm FROM THE EXTERNAL SURFACE

RESULTS (all in mW/cm2, the unit used by both regulations — no conversion applied)

  (a) Canada, Radiation Emitting Devices Regulations, C.R.C., c. 1370, Sch. II, Part III, s. 4(1)(a)(i), with the prescribed test load in place ............ 1.0 mW/cm2
  (b) US, 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1), measured prior to acquisition by a purchaser ............ 1 mW/cm2
  (c) US, 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1), thereafter (after acquisition by a purchaser) ............ 5 mW/cm2

Binding number for a new oven shipped to both markets: 1.0 mW/cm2 (asks (a) and (b) are numerically identical: 1.0 = 1). The 5 mW/cm2 US post-sale figure is an in-use ceiling, not a manufacturing-release criterion, and is 5x looser.


1. SCOPE AND SOURCES CONSULTED (currency stated so the reader can re-verify)

  Canada: Radiation Emitting Devices Regulations, C.R.C., c. 1370, made under the Radiation Emitting Devices Act; consolidation current to 2026-10-29, last amended 2025-10-09 (https://laws.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/C.R.C.,_c._1370/FullText.html). The microwave-oven provisions sit in Schedule II, Part III (sections 2-4 and the standards of functioning in s. 4).
  United States: 21 CFR 1030.10, 'Microwave ovens' (performance standard under 21 U.S.C. 360kk / Radiation Control for Health and Safety Act). Verified against the eCFR current text and the 2025 annual print (govinfo, CFR-2025-title21-vol8, sec. 1030-10); the two are word-for-word identical on the power-density provision quoted below.
  Both texts were read directly, not from summaries; the numbers below are quoted from the operative sentences.


2. CANADA — ASK (a)

Operative text, s. 4(1) (Schedule II, Part III):
  '4 (1) Every microwave oven shall, when fully assembled and operating with its service controls and user controls adjusted to yield the maximum output, function in such a manner that
   (a) the leakage radiation, measured with the instrument prescribed by paragraph (3)(b), at all points at least 5 cm from the external surface of the oven, does not exceed
     (i) 1.0 mW/cm2 with the test load prescribed by paragraph (3)(a) placed
       (A) in the centre of the shelf in the cavity, in the case of an oven that is designed for cooking and that has a total microwave power generating capacity not greater than 1.5 kW, and
       (B) as specified by the manufacturer, in the case of an oven other than an oven described in clause (A), and
     (ii) 5.0 mW/cm2 without a test load, where the oven is operable in such conditions...'

ANSWER (a): 1.0 mW/cm2, measured with the prescribed test load in place.

Prescribed conditions that travel with that number (s. 4(3)):
  - Test load, cooking oven <= 1.5 kW total microwave power generating capacity: 275 +/- 15 mL of water at an initial temperature of 20 +/- 5 C, placed in the centre of the shelf in the cavity.
  - Test load, any other oven: the substance and amount specified by the manufacturer as the test load.
  - Instrument: capable of measuring a power density of 1.0 mW/cm2 with an accuracy of 2 dB or better, and with an indicator response time not greater than 3 seconds.
  - Oven state: fully assembled, service and user controls adjusted to yield maximum output.
  - Geometry: all points at least 5 cm from the external surface ('external surface' is defined in the Part III definitions as the outside surface of the manufacturer's cabinet/enclosure, including doors, door handles, latches and control knobs).

Deliberately NOT the answer to (a), but present in the same section and easy to mis-cite:
  - s. 4(1)(a)(ii): 5.0 mW/cm2 WITHOUT a test load, where the oven is operable in such conditions. This is a separate, no-load condition.
  - s. 4(2): 5.0 mW/cm2 with the outer enclosure removed, measured at all points at least 5 cm from every user-accessible mechanical or electronic part. This is a service/design condition, not the normal-operation leakage limit.
  - s. 4(1)(b): X-ray exposure at 5 cm not to exceed 0.5 mR per hour over 10 cm2 — a different quantity (exposure rate, not power density).


3. UNITED STATES — ASKS (b) AND (c)

Operative text, 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1):
  '(c) Requirements — (1) Power density limit. The equivalent plane-wave power density existing in the proximity of the external oven surface shall not exceed 1 milliwatt per square centimeter at any point 5 centimeters or more from the external surface of the oven, measured prior to acquisition by a purchaser, and, thereafter, 5 milliwatts per square centimeter at any such point.'

ANSWER (b): 1 mW/cm2 — the limit that applies to an oven measured prior to acquisition by a purchaser (i.e., the manufacturer's release/pre-market condition).
ANSWER (c): 5 mW/cm2 — the limit that applies 'thereafter', i.e., once the oven has been acquired by a purchaser and is in use.

Definitions that fix the measurand (21 CFR 1030.10(b)):
  - 'External surface' = the outside surface of the cabinet or enclosure provided by the manufacturer as part of the microwave oven, including doors, door handles, latches and control knobs.
  - 'Equivalent plane-wave power density' = the square of the rms electric field strength divided by the impedance of free space (377 ohms). This is what the 'mW/cm2' figure means in the US rule; it is not SAR and not a food-heating quantity.

Measurement and test conditions (21 CFR 1030.10(c)(3)) that must accompany either number:
  - Instrument must reach 90 percent of its steady-state reading within 3 seconds under a step-function input.
  - Tests must account for all measurement errors and uncertainties so that the equivalent plane-wave power density does not exceed the applicable limit (i.e., measured value + uncertainty <= limit).
  - Compliance is judged on the maximum reading at the location of greatest emission, measured through at least one stirrer cycle; alternative procedures may be requested under 21 CFR 1010.13 where stirrer characteristics make the standard procedure unsuitable.
  - Related but separate: 21 CFR 1030.10(e) recommends a leakage check on each oven prior to release to the owner — an operational practice supporting the 1 mW/cm2 pre-acquisition limit, not a third numeric limit.


4. SIDE-BY-SIDE SUMMARY TABLE

  Jurisdiction / stage                              | Limit (mW/cm2) | Distance     | Load
  -------------------------------------------------|----------------|--------------|----------------------------------
  Canada, s. 4(1)(a)(i), with test load           | 1.0            | >= 5 cm      | 275 +/- 15 mL water, 20 +/- 5 C (cooking oven <= 1.5 kW); centre of shelf
  US, 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1), pre-acquisition        | 1              | >= 5 cm      | Standard does not itself prescribe a load in (c)(1); the emission is the equivalent plane-wave power density through >= 1 stirrer cycle
  US, 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1), after acquisition     | 5              | >= 5 cm      | as above (in-use ceiling)
  [Canada, s. 4(1)(a)(ii), no test load — not asked]| 5.0           | >= 5 cm      | none
  [Canada, s. 4(2), enclosure removed — not asked] | 5.0            | >= 5 cm      | test load per 4(3)(a)


5. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR A SINGLE OVEN MODEL SOLD IN BOTH COUNTRIES

  - The pre-market limits in the two countries coincide exactly at 1.0 mW/cm2 (Canada) and 1 mW/cm2 (US). A single design and a single type-test dataset can therefore demonstrate both, provided the Canadian load (275 +/- 15 mL water at 20 +/- 5 C) is in place and the survey covers all points at least 5 cm from the external surface with controls at maximum output.
  - Design/release target: demonstrate <= 1.0 mW/cm2 with uncertainty included. Because Canada permits instrument accuracy of 2 dB (a power ratio of 10^0.2 = 1.585) and the US requires all measurement errors and uncertainties to be accounted for, a defensible guard-banded release target is 1.0 / 1.585 = 0.63 mW/cm2 (measured, worst point), i.e. design to about 0.6 mW/cm2. This is a recommendation, not a regulatory figure, and it sits below both 1.0 mW/cm2 limits — it cannot conflict with them.
  - The US post-acquisition 5 mW/cm2 value does not relax the release requirement. An oven must still leave the factory at or below 1 mW/cm2; the 5 mW/cm2 figure only defines the in-service ceiling after a purchaser takes delivery (relevant to servicing, field leakage checks, and post-repair verification).
  - Do not use the Canadian 5.0 mW/cm2 no-load or enclosure-removed figures as a market-entry criterion: neither corresponds to the normal-operation, loaded condition asked about here.


6. HOW TO REPRODUCE THE MEASUREMENT (so the stated numbers are auditable)

  1) Assemble the oven fully; install the prescribed load — 275 +/- 15 mL of water at 20 +/- 5 C in the centre of the shelf for a cooking oven of <= 1.5 kW total microwave power generating capacity; otherwise the manufacturer-specified load.
  2) Set service and user controls to yield maximum output.
  3) Use a leakage instrument meeting both requirements: capable of measuring 1.0 mW/cm2 to 2 dB or better with <= 3 s indicator response (Canada s. 4(3)(b)), and reaching 90 percent of steady-state within 3 s (US 1030.10(c)(3)(i)).
  4) Survey the entire external surface at a standoff of at least 5 cm, including door seams, hinges, latches, control panel, waveguide/magnetron access panels and vents; probe orientation per the instrument manufacturer's calibration.
  5) Observe through at least one complete stirrer cycle (US) and record the maximum reading at the point of greatest emission.
  6) Add the measurement uncertainty to the maximum reading and compare against 1.0 mW/cm2 (both countries, pre-market). Report the worst-point value, the uncertainty budget, the load actually used, and the instrument calibration date.


7. LIMITS OF THIS DETERMINATION

  - These are emission (leakage) limits for the device; they are not occupational or general-public exposure limits (e.g., Health Canada Safety Code 6 or FCC/IC RF exposure rules) and should not be substituted for them.
  - The Canadian figures are from the consolidation current to 2026-10-29; the US figures are from the 2025 annual print and current eCFR. Re-verify currency at the time of filing: the Canadian regulation was amended in 2025, and although s. 4(1)(a)(i) is quoted verbatim from the current consolidation, a future amendment could change the numbering even if the limit is unchanged.
  - Nothing here addresses the Canadian administrative requirements (registration/licensing, labelling under s. 3, the 'CAUTION — MICROWAVES / ATTENTION — MICRO-ONDES' marking) or the US reporting/recordkeeping obligations in 21 CFR Part 1002 and the certification requirements of 21 CFR Part 1010; those are separate compliance workstreams.

question: X30
shape: Occupational noise exposure limits, Canadian federal workplaces
answer:
DETERMINATION — MAXIMUM DAILY EXPOSURE AT 93 dBA AND THE L(ex,8) CEILING
Canada Occupational Health and Safety Regulations, SOR/86-304, Part VII (Levels of Sound), ss. 7.1–7.4 and the Schedule to s. 7.4. Consolidation current to 2026-10-29, last amended 2025-03-26.

1. SCOPE AND REGULATORY BASIS
- Governing instrument: the Canada Occupational Health and Safety Regulations (COHSR), SOR/86-304, Part VII, made under the Canada Labour Code, Part II. This is the general federal workplace regime.
- Excluded, per the request: the marine-vessel regime (the Maritime Occupational Health and Safety Regulations) and the offshore oil and gas regimes (the Canada–Newfoundland and Labrador Offshore Area and Canada–Nova Scotia Offshore Area occupational health and safety regulations made under the Atlantic Accord Acts). Those instruments carry their own noise tables and limits; nothing from them is used below.
- Section 7.4 imposes two independent limits, both of which must be satisfied in any 24-hour period:
  (a) an A-weighted sound pressure level listed in column I of the Schedule must not be experienced for longer than the duration in column II; and
  (b) the noise exposure level L(ex,8) must not exceed 87 dBA.
  These are cumulative, not alternatives: whichever binds first governs. In this case they bind at the same point.

2. LIMIT 1 — LONGEST PERMITTED EXPOSURE AT A STEADY 93 dBA
- The Schedule to s. 7.4 runs from 87 dBA to 120 dBA in 3 dB steps, with the permitted duration halving at each step: 87 dBA / 8 h; 90 dBA / 4 h; 93 dBA / 2 h; 96 dBA / 1 h; and so on with sub-hour durations to 120 dBA.
- 93 dBA falls exactly on a tabulated row. Column II for 93 dBA is 2 hours.
- ANSWER: the longest permitted exposure at a steady 93 dBA is 2 hours per employee per 24-hour period.
- Independent derivation from s. 7.4(b) and the s. 7.1 definition of noise exposure level (L(ex,8) = 10 log10 of the time integral of squared A-weighted sound pressure over any 24-hour period, divided by 8, reference pressure 20 uPa): for a steady level L held for T hours, L(ex,8) = L + 10 log10(T/8). Setting L(ex,8) = 87 dBA and L = 93 dBA:
    T_max = 8 x 10^(-(93-87)/10) = 8 x 10^(-0.6) = 8 x 0.2512 = 2.01 h.
  The Schedule's 2 h is therefore the binding and very slightly conservative figure; use 2 h, not 2.01 h.
- Levels between tabulated rows: apply the duration for the next lower tabulated level. Never round a measured level down or interpolate to a longer duration.

3. LIMIT 2 — CEILING ON THE 8-HOUR-NORMALISED NOISE EXPOSURE LEVEL
- s. 7.4(b) prohibits exposure in any 24-hour period to a noise exposure level (L(ex,8)) that exceeds 87 dBA.
- ANSWER: the separate ceiling on L(ex,8) is 87 dBA.
- Properties to apply: it is separate from the per-level Schedule limit; it applies regardless of how the dose is accumulated (one steady level, or many short exposures); it is normalised to 8 hours, so it is not raised for a 10- or 12-hour shift; and it cannot be satisfied by wearing hearing protectors, because compliance is assessed on the sound field at the employee's ear.

4. CONSISTENCY CHECK OF THE TWO LIMITS AT 93 dBA
Hours at 93 dBA -> L(ex,8) -> status against the 87 dBA ceiling:
  0.5 h -> 80.97 dBA -> permitted
  1.0 h -> 83.97 dBA -> permitted
  1.5 h -> 85.72 dBA -> permitted
  2.0 h -> 86.99 dBA -> permitted (equals the ceiling within rounding; not an exceedance)
  2.5 h -> 87.96 dBA -> NOT permitted (violates 7.4(b))
  3.0 h -> 88.74 dBA -> NOT permitted (violates 7.4(b))
The Schedule value (2 h) and the ceiling value (87 dBA) are mutually consistent: 2 h at 93 dBA lands exactly on 87 dBA. No figure stated in this determination exceeds a limit stated in this determination.

5. AGGREGATION OVER THE 24-HOUR PERIOD
- Formula (all A-weighted levels at or above 74 dBA must be included per s. 7.2(3); levels below 74 dBA may be included per s. 7.2(4)):
    L(ex,8) = 10 log10 [ (1/8) x SUM_i ( T_i x 10^(L_i/10) ) ],  T_i in hours.
- Equivalent dose budget: SUM_i ( T_i x 10^(L_i/10) ) must not exceed 8 x 10^8.7 = 4.01 x 10^9 (units of 10^(L/10) x hours).
- Check: 2.0 h at 93 dBA consumes 2 x 10^9.3 = 3.99 x 10^9, i.e. 99.6 percent of the budget. Any additional exposure at 74 dBA or above in the same 24 hours therefore pushes the employee over the ceiling, so time at 93 dBA must be reduced accordingly.
- Worked mixed example: 1.0 h at 93 dBA plus 5.0 h at 82 dBA gives L(ex,8) = 10 log10[(10^9.3 + 5 x 10^8.2)/8] = 10 log10(3.48 x 10^8) = 85.4 dBA — compliant, with headroom.
- The limit applies to any 24-hour period, not the calendar day. Aggregate across split shifts, call-outs, second jobs and on-call time within a rolling 24-hour window.

6. MEASUREMENT AND VERIFICATION REQUIREMENTS
- Instrument and method: s. 7.2 requires measurement by an instrument recommended for that purpose in clause 4.3 of CSA CAN/CSA-Z107.56-13 (Measurement of Noise Exposure) and meeting the clause 4 requirements; measurement must follow clauses 5, 6.4.1, 6.4.4, 6.5.2, 6.5.4, 6.6.2 and 6.6.4 of that Standard. The s. 7.1 definition requires a sound level meter meeting IEC 651 (1979) Type 2 performance with an IEC 651 A-weighting filter.
- For a claimed steady 93 dBA: verify with a Type 1 or Type 2 sound level meter on slow response at the ear position (or in the space the employee occupies), plus personal dosimetry for a full shift where the task mix or position varies. Calibrate with an acoustic calibrator before and after; record windscreen, microphone position/orientation, measurement duration, and the exact task steps covered.
- Instrument uncertainty matters here. Type 2 instruments and field conditions give roughly plus or minus 1–2 dB; at 93 dBA a 2 dB error changes the permitted time by a factor of about 1.6 (from 1.26 h to 3.2 h). Do not schedule to the exact limit on the strength of a single spot reading.

7. DUTIES TRIGGERED BY THIS EXPOSURE (Part VII)
- s. 7.3(1): where an employee may be exposed to 84 dBA or more for a duration likely to endanger hearing, the employer must without delay appoint a qualified person to investigate the degree of exposure and notify the workplace committee or health and safety representative. A steady 93 dBA triggers this.
- The s. 7.3 investigation report must contain observations and recommendations to ensure compliance with ss. 7.4 to 7.8, including recommendations on hearing protectors; it must be kept at the workplace for ten years after its date (s. 7.3(6)).
- s. 7.3(5)(c): recommendations respecting hearing protectors for employees exposed to L(ex,8) at or above 84 dBA and not above 87 dBA.
- s. 7.3(7): where the report states an employee is likely to be exposed to L(ex,8) of 84 dBA or more, post the report conspicuously and give the employee written information describing the hazards of high sound levels.
- s. 7.5: where a limit is exceeded, reduce exposure — engineering and administrative controls first (source enclosure, silencers/mufflers, vibration isolation and damping, moving the noisy task away from the operator, automating the task, limiting time on task, rotating staff).
- Hearing protectors: required where the limits are exceeded, but never credited in the s. 7.4 comparison. Compliance is judged on the exposure at the ear without protection; protectors are an additional safeguard, not a substitute for the limit.
- Hearing conservation follow-through: audiometric testing and the remaining Part VII duties (ss. 7.6–7.8 and related provisions), noise warning signage at the boundary of the area, and training on the hazards and on correct protector use.

8. NOTE ON IMPULSIVE NOISE
COHSR Part VII as retrieved contains no separate C-weighted peak limit (unlike some provincial regimes, e.g. British Columbia's 140 dBC). If the 93 dBA is not in fact steady — impacts, bangs, drops, pneumatic discharge — the s. 7.4 limits still apply and must be measured per CSA Z107.56-13, which addresses impulsive noise. Confirm the steady assumption with peak and impulse settings on the meter and document it before relying on the 2-hour figure.

9. PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATION
Because 2 h at 93 dBA lands exactly on the 87 dBA ceiling, there is zero margin for measurement error or overrun. Unless the level and time on task are tightly controlled and verified by dosimetry, set an administrative cap of 1.5 h per 24 h at 93 dBA (L(ex,8) = 85.7 dBA), require hearing protectors for any residual time in the area, and post the area as a noise hazard.

10. ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITS OF THIS DETERMINATION
- The 93 dBA is steady, continuous and A-weighted at the employee's ear for the whole of the stated exposure, with no impulsive component and no significant additional exposure at or above 74 dBA in the same 24 hours beyond what is computed above.
- Current consolidation of SOR/86-304 applies; no variance, exemption or approval alters the s. 7.4 limits.
- No credit is taken for hearing protection or for administrative controls in the compliance comparison.
- The Schedule row for 93 dBA is 2 h; the value is independently confirmed at 2.01 h by s. 7.4(b) with the s. 7.1 definition of L(ex,8), so the answer does not rest on the table alone.

question: X31
shape: Radiocommunications licensing, Australia (ACMA low-interference-potential-devices class licence)
answer:
ANSWER TO ASK 5 (year of making of the instrument in force on 17 November 2026): 2025.

The instrument in force on 17 November 2026 is the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025 (Federal Register of Legislation ID F2025L01047), administered by the Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts under the Radiocommunications Act 1992. Evidence: the FRL record shows the title 'Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025', status 'In force', registered 05 September 2025. The ACMA consultation/outcomes page for the remake states the predecessor licence 'is due to sunset on 1 October 2025' and that the ACMA 'decided to proceed with making the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025. The instrument will commence on 1 October 2025.' Therefore from 1 October 2025 — and hence on 17 November 2026 — the 2025 licence, not the 2015 licence, is the operative class licence, and the year carried in its name (and the year of its making/registration) is 2025.

Trap to record explicitly: '2016' is not the year of the class licence. F2016L00636 is the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence Variation 2016 (No.1), which was in force only 03 May 2016 – 04 May 2016 and is now repealed. It was a variation instrument, not the class licence. Likewise the 2015 licence (F2015L01438) is shown on the FRL as 'No longer in force'. Any answer of 2015 or 2016 for ask 5 is wrong as at 17 November 2026.

WHAT THE 2025 REMAKE CHANGED (from the ACMA outcomes page), for context only: new arrangements for wireless audio transmitters using WMAS in 520–694 MHz; frequency-hopping transmitters in 5925–6425 MHz; digital modulation transmitters in 5150–5250 MHz; RLAN transmitters in 6425–6585 MHz; radiodetermination transmitters in 13.4–14 GHz and 76–77 GHz. The 2400–2483.5 MHz digital modulation entry is NOT listed among the changes, which makes verbatim carry-over from the 2015 licence the most likely outcome — but likelihood is not verification (see blocked asks).

ASKS 2 AND 4 — NOT ANSWERED, AND WHY.
The maximum EIRP (in watts) for a 'digital modulation' radiocommunications transmitter in 2400–2483.5 MHz, and the additional radiated peak power spectral density limit attaching to that class, both live in the Schedule 1 transmitter table of the 2025 instrument. That table was not retrieved. The available sources establish only: the instrument's identity, its registration (05 Sep 2025), its commencement (1 Oct 2025), and the list of bands whose arrangements changed. They do not contain the 2.4 GHz digital modulation row, its EIRP column value, or its conditions column. Rather than assert a number on paper, both are recorded as blocked.

UNVERIFIED EXPECTATION (do not use for a compliance statement, do not put on a product label or in a supplier declaration): secondary sources commonly cite the 2015 licence's 2400–2483.5 MHz digital modulation entry as 4 W EIRP (36 dBm), with a radiated peak PSD condition attached, and the phrasing of the question presupposes that a PSD limit exists for this class. Treat that as a hypothesis to be tested against the 2025 Schedule, not as the answer. I am deliberately not stating a PSD figure: the bandwidth basis and reference plane are exactly the details most likely to have changed or to be misremembered.

VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (to close both blocked asks in one pass):
1. Open https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2025L01047/asmade/text and download the as-made legislative instrument (PDF/Word). Use the as-made text, or the latest compilation if one exists at the date of use; note the compilation number and date in the compliance file, because a compilation after 17 Nov 2026 would not describe the law as at that date.
2. Read the definitions section. Record the instrument's own definitions of: 'EIRP' (and whether it is a radiated/antenna-referenced quantity), 'digital modulation radiocommunications transmitter' (or equivalent class name), and 'radiated peak power spectral density' including its stated measurement bandwidth and detector.
3. Locate Schedule 1 (Transmitters). Find every row whose frequency band covers any part of 2400–2483.5 MHz. Expect several overlapping rows (e.g. digital modulation, frequency hopping, RLAN, generic low-power devices).
4. Apply the instrument's own overlap rule. Class licences of this type typically provide that where more than one item could apply, the transmitter must comply with the item that applies to it as a matter of its type, and where two items both apply, the more restrictive limit governs; confirm the actual wording rather than assuming.
5. From the digital modulation row for 2400–2483.5 MHz, record verbatim: the maximum EIRP (and whether stated in W, mW, dBm or dBW); the conditions column in full, including any PSD limit, any bandwidth or minimum-hop/dwell condition, any duty-cycle or power-control condition, and any indoor-only or antenna restriction.
6. Convert to watts using the table below and record both the native expression and the converted value, e.g. '4 W EIRP (36 dBm) as stated in item N'.
7. Re-check the ACMA website for any variation to the 2025 licence registered between 1 Oct 2025 and 17 Nov 2026, and confirm none alters the 2.4 GHz digital modulation row.

dBm → watts conversions (P(W) = 10^((dBm−30)/10)):
 36 dBm = 4.000 W | 33 dBm = 1.995 W | 30 dBm = 1.000 W | 27 dBm = 0.501 W | 24 dBm = 0.251 W | 23 dBm = 0.200 W | 20 dBm = 0.100 W | 17 dBm = 0.050 W | 10 dBm = 0.010 W | 0 dBm = 0.001 W.
dBW → watts: 6 dBW = 3.981 W | 5 dBW = 3.162 W | 0 dBW = 1.000 W | −10 dBW = 0.100 W.
PSD conversions: a limit of X dBm per bandwidth B is X dBm in B; to express per MHz, add 10·log10(1 MHz / B) if B < 1 MHz, subtract if B > 1 MHz (e.g. 36 dBm per 8 MHz = 36 + 10·log10(1/8) = 36 − 9.03 = 26.97 dBm/MHz; 10 dBm per MHz = 10 + 10·log10(8) = 19.03 dBm per 8 MHz). Keep the native expression in the compliance file; do not convert a PSD limit into a different bandwidth basis for a declaration.

DESIGN CONSEQUENCE PENDING VERIFICATION (for the hardware workstream): the 2.4 GHz RF chain, antenna gain budget and conducted-power setpoint cannot be frozen until the Schedule row is read, because the binding constraint could be either the total EIRP ceiling or the peak-PSD ceiling depending on occupied bandwidth. For a wideband (≥8 MHz) digital-modulation link the total-EIRP ceiling normally binds; for a narrowband emission the PSD ceiling binds and the permitted total EIRP is much lower than the headline figure. Design the front end with a conducted-power setpoint plus antenna gain that satisfies the PSD limit across the narrowest occupied bandwidth the modem can be configured to, and add a manufacturing test step that measures peak PSD in the licence's stated bandwidth, not just total power. Class licences are non-discretionary: operation is authorised only if every condition of the entry is met, so the EIRP figure alone is never the compliance criterion.

question: X32
shape: Occupational noise, Great Britain statutory instrument
answer:
ANSWER TO THE EMPLOYER (Great Britain, manufacturing)

Legal instrument: The Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, SI 2005/1643 (E+W+S), reg 4. These are the GB-wide general noise regulations for manufacturing; no devolved variation applies and no sector-specific regime is engaged.

1. LEGAL EXPOSURE LIMIT VALUES (reg 4(3)) — these must not be exceeded
   (a) daily or weekly personal noise exposure: 87 dB(A)
   (b) peak sound pressure: 140 dB(C)

   Full reg 4 table, for context:
   | Level | Daily/weekly personal exposure | Peak sound pressure |
   |---|---|---|
   | Lower exposure action value — reg 4(1) | 80 dB(A) | 135 dB(C) |
   | Upper exposure action value — reg 4(2) | 85 dB(A) | 137 dB(C) |
   | Exposure limit value — reg 4(3) | 87 dB(A) | 140 dB(C) |

   Notes on the values:
   - 'Daily or weekly personal noise exposure' is LEX,8h or, where reg 4(4) is used, LEX,40h, ascertained under Schedule 1; peak sound pressure is the maximum C-weighted instantaneous sound pressure ascertained under Schedule 2. Peak is not averaged.
   - Weekly averaging (reg 4(4)) is available only where exposure varies markedly from day to day; it is a choice, not a default.
   - The limit values are absolute. There is no 'so far as is reasonably practicable' qualification on reg 4(3): a breach is a breach.
   - The limit values are not targets. Because the protection actually delivered by hearing protectors is uncertain, exposure should be controlled by engineering and organisational measures (reg 6) to below the upper exposure action value, not merely to below 87 dB(A).

2. MAY HEARING PROTECTOR ATTENUATION BE COUNTED AGAINST THE UPPER EXPOSURE ACTION VALUE? — NO

   Reg 4(5) is decisive and reads: 'In applying the exposure limit values in paragraph (3), but not in applying the lower and upper exposure action values in paragraphs (1) and (2), account shall be taken of the protection given to the employee by any personal hearing protectors provided by the employer in accordance with regulation 7(2).'

   Therefore:
   - When deciding whether the upper exposure action value (85 dB(A) or 137 dB(C)) is reached or exceeded, the employer must use the exposure the employee would receive WITHOUT credit for hearing protection. Protector attenuation is irrelevant to that judgement.
   - Protector attenuation is counted only in the separate exercise of checking compliance with the exposure limit values (87 dB(A) or 140 dB(C)), i.e. the level at the ear of a protected employee.
   - It follows that an argument of the form 'measured 92 dB(A), issued 25 dB muffs, so exposure is 67 dB(A) and we are below 85 dB(A)' is wrong in law. The upper action value is reached at 92 dB(A) and all the reg 7(2)/7(3) duties bite.

3. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE — WHAT THE EMPLOYER MUST DO

   Step 1 (reg 5): assess exposure without hearing protection. Use measured LEX,8h/LEX,40h and peak dB(C).

   Step 2: compare the unprotected values with the action values.
   - ≥ 80 dB(A) or ≥ 135 dB(C) (lower EAV): reg 7(1) — make personal hearing protectors available on request; reg 9 health surveillance for those at risk; reg 10 information, instruction and training.
   - ≥ 85 dB(A) or ≥ 137 dB(C) (upper EAV): reg 6(3) — reduce exposure by means other than hearing protection so far as is reasonably practicable; reg 7(2) — provide personal hearing protectors (mandatory, not on request) to any employee so exposed where the employer cannot by other means reduce exposure below the upper EAV; reg 7(3) — designate and demarcate a Hearing Protection Zone with the mandatory ear-protection sign (Health and Safety (Safety Signs and Signals) Regulations 1996, Sch 1 Part II para 3.3), restrict access where practicable and justified, and ensure so far as is reasonably practicable that no one enters unless wearing protectors; reg 9 — health surveillance; reg 10 — information, instruction and training.
   - Protectors must be selected (reg 7(4)) so as to eliminate the risk to hearing or reduce it to as low a level as is reasonably practicable, after consultation with employees or their representatives, and maintained in efficient condition.

   Step 3 (limit-value check only): having issued protectors, calculate the exposure at the ear of the protected employee and check it against 87 dB(A) and 140 dB(C). This is the ONLY point at which attenuation enters the calculation. If the at-ear exposure still exceeds 87 dB(A) or 140 dB(C), the exposure limit value is being exceeded and the employer is in breach of reg 4(3) — further control (usually engineering) is required.

4. HOW TO ESTIMATE ATTENUATION WHEN IT IS USED (limit-value check only)

   Use the protector manufacturer's data and the methods in HSE L108 'Controlling noise at work':
   - Preferred: octave-band assumed protection values (APV), L'A = L_oct − APV per band, summed.
   - Alternative: HML method.
   - Simplest: SNR method, L'A ≈ L_A − (SNR − 5) (equivalently L'A = L_C − SNR). This is known to over-estimate protection in many real situations; apply a safety margin and prefer the octave-band method where the answer matters. (Method choice and any margin are HSE guidance, not law; the legal requirement is only that 'account shall be taken of the protection given'.)
   - Do not use laboratory SNR/MWN figures uncritically as the real-world performance: fit, wear time, comfort, spectacle arms, hair and beard all degrade protection. Real-world protection is commonly 10–20 dB below the labelled figure.

   Worked example (illustrative only, not a site assessment): measured unprotected LEX,8h = 93 dB(A), peak = 141 dB(C). Upper EAV exceeded on both counts → protectors mandatory (reg 7(2)), Hearing Protection Zone required (reg 7(3)). Limit check with an earmuff of SNR 26 dB: L'A ≈ 93 − (26 − 5) = 72 dB(A), below 87 dB(A); peak at ear, using octave-band data (say ~20 dB at the dominant frequency), ≈ 121 dB(C), below 140 dB(C). Compliance with the limit values is achieved — but the employee's exposure for action-value purposes remains 93 dB(A)/141 dB(C), and the 72 dB(A) figure must never be reported as the exposure or used to argue that the action values are not reached.

5. COMMON ERRORS TO AVOID
   - Counting protector attenuation against the lower or upper exposure action values (prohibited by reg 4(5)).
   - Treating 87 dB(A) as the design target and relying on protectors instead of reducing noise at source.
   - Applying weekly averaging where exposure does not vary markedly day to day, to bring a high daily exposure under an action value.
   - Rounding an assessed 84.6 dB(A) up or an 85.4 dB(A) down to avoid triggering duties; compare the actual assessed values, and where there is doubt resolve it in favour of protection.
   - Assuming the peak value is averaged over the day; it is the single maximum.

6. SCOPE AND CAVEATS
   - This is a statement of the legal requirements and their application to a manufacturing employer in Great Britain. It is not a site-specific compliance assessment: the employer must still measure/assess its own exposures under reg 5 and determine which action values are reached.
   - Enforcement is by HSE or the local authority; breach of reg 4 (and of the action-value duties) is an offence under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, s.33.
   - Transitional commencement arrangements that applied to the music and entertainment sectors do not affect a manufacturing employer and are not considered here.

question: X33
shape: Occupational exposure limits, UK HSE EH40/2005
answer:
CARBON MONOXIDE — EH40/2005 WELs AND STATUS OF THE TRANSITIONAL HIGHER PAIR

1. ANSWERS

| # | Ask | Answer |
|---|-----|--------|
| 1 | Long-term (8-h TWA) WEL, ppm | 20 ppm (23 mg.m-3) |
| 2 | Short-term (15-min) WEL, ppm | 100 ppm (117 mg.m-3) |
| 3 | To whom the second, higher pair applied | Underground mining and tunnelling industries ONLY |
| 4 | Does that higher pair still apply on 17 November 2026? | No — it expired on 21 August 2023 |

The second, higher pair was 30 ppm (35 mg.m-3) 8-h TWA and 200 ppm (232 mg.m-3) 15-min STEL.

2. SOURCE AND EXACT ENTRY

Source: HSE, EH40/2005 Workplace exposure limits, Fourth edition 2020 (ISBN 978 0 7176 6733 8), Table 1 'List of approved workplace exposure limits', entry:

  Carbon monoxide | CAS 630-08-0 | LTEL 20 ppm / 23 mg.m-3 | STEL 100 ppm / 117 mg.m-3 | LTEL 30 ppm / 35 mg.m-3 | STEL 200 ppm / 232 mg.m-3 | Comments: 'BMGV' and 'Limits applicable to underground mining & tunnelling industries ONLY until 21/8/23'

Table 1 has a two-tier column structure — ppm and mg.m-3 under each of the long-term (8-hr TWA reference period) and short-term (15-minute reference period) headings — and the carbon monoxide entry is a two-sub-row entry. Resolved by column, not by reading order, the entry is:

  Sub-row A (general WEL):     LTEL 20 ppm = 23 mg.m-3;  STEL 100 ppm = 117 mg.m-3
  Sub-row B (transitional):    LTEL 30 ppm = 35 mg.m-3;  STEL 200 ppm = 232 mg.m-3

Sub-row B carries the qualifying comment 'Limits applicable to underground mining & tunnelling industries ONLY until 21/8/23'. The capitalised 'ONLY' is HSE's own emphasis.

Corroboration: UKHSA 'Compendium of chemical hazards: carbon monoxide' (GOV-12238, published May 2022), Table 5 'Occupational standards', cites EH40/2005 Fourth Edition (2020) and prints the identical structure — WEL 20 ppm / 23 mg.m-3 and 100 ppm / 117 mg.m-3, plus 'Limits applicable to underground mining and tunnelling industries only until 21 August 2023' at 30 ppm / 35 mg.m-3 and 200 ppm / 232 mg.m-3.

3. INTERNAL CONSISTENCY CHECK (unit cross-verification)

Using mg.m-3 = ppm x (28.01 / 24.05) = ppm x 1.1646 at 20 C and 101.3 kPa:

  20 x 1.1646 = 23.3  -> printed 23   OK
  30 x 1.1646 = 34.9  -> printed 35   OK
  100 x 1.1646 = 116.5 -> printed 117 OK
  200 x 1.1646 = 232.9 -> printed 232 OK

All four mg.m-3 figures reconcile with their ppm partners, which confirms the ppm/mg.m-3 column assignment above and rules out a column transposition. The two ppm values reported in results (20 and 100) are the general WEL sub-row, not the transitional sub-row.

4. THE SECOND, HIGHER PAIR — WHO IT APPLIED TO

It applied to work in the underground mining and tunnelling industries only. It was a sector-specific transitional derogation, not a general limit: for those industries alone, the 8-h TWA limit was 30 ppm instead of 20 ppm and the 15-min STEL was 200 ppm instead of 100 ppm. Outside those industries the higher pair never applied — the 20 ppm / 100 ppm WEL applied to every other sector throughout.

Context (interpretive, not a quotation from EH40): such transitional values are granted where the general limit is not achievable with available control technology in a defined sector — in this case diesel plant and blasting fumes in confined headings — and are time-limited so that controls must be improved rather than the derogation becoming permanent.

5. DOES IT STILL APPLY ON 17 NOVEMBER 2026? — NO

The comment fixes the end point as 21/8/23, i.e. 21 August 2023. That date passed 3 years and 3 months before the stated 'today' of 17 November 2026. The transitional pair therefore has no legal or advisory effect on that date, and there is no renewal mechanism in the entry — the value simply ceases to be a WEL.

Consequence: since 22 August 2023 there has been a single carbon monoxide WEL applying to all sectors, including underground mining and tunnelling:

  8-hr TWA: 20 ppm (23 mg.m-3)
  15-min STEL: 100 ppm (117 mg.m-3)

Any CO assessment in a mine or tunnel dated on or after 22 August 2023 must be judged against 20 ppm / 100 ppm. A 30 ppm TWA or a 200 ppm 15-minute peak is now an exceedance in those industries, not a compliant result.

Currency of the edition: the HSE catalogue page for EH40/2005 (page updated 26 February 2026) still offers the Fourth edition 2020 (published January 2020, ISBN 9780717667031) as the current text, and HSE's standing note states that 'the WELs listed in Table 1 of EH40/2005 supersede any WELs contained in other HSE guidance or publications'. Nothing in the retrieved material shows any post-2020 amendment altering the carbon monoxide entry; the 2020 changes (13 new/revised WELs from 17 January 2020, from Directive (EU) 2017/2398) did not include carbon monoxide. The answer is therefore not sensitive to which side of 17 November 2026 the check is made, because the operative event (21 August 2023) is in the past.

6. PRACTICAL APPLICATION NOTES (occupational hygiene)

- Comparison basis: personal 8-hour TWA sampling compared with 20 ppm; 15-minute samples (or direct-reading instrument peaks) compared with 100 ppm. The STEL is a 15-minute reference period and must not be exceeded at any point in the shift; the 8-h TWA is calculated per the EH40 Schedule (sum of C x T over 8 hours).
- Direct-reading instruments (electrochemical CO cells) are the normal tool for the 15-minute comparison, with a data-logging interval of 1 minute or less so that genuine 15-minute averages can be constructed.
- Biological monitoring: the carbon monoxide row carries the 'BMGV' notation, meaning EH40 also publishes a biological monitoring guidance value for CO in Table 2. Read the numeric BMGV and its specified sampling time directly from Table 2 of the current edition — the retrieved passage records the notation only, not the figure, and it should not be quoted from memory. Note that a BMGV is a guidance value indicating good practice, not a WEL, and compliance with it does not by itself demonstrate compliance with the airborne WEL.
- Do not rely on secondary summaries for this substance. The 30 ppm / 200 ppm pair is still reproduced in older guidance and in the 2022 UKHSA compendium as a historical record; it is expired and must not be used as a current limit.
- Jurisdiction: the answer is for Great Britain under COSHH 2002 (as amended), for which EH40 Table 1 is the approved list. Northern Ireland has its own COSHH(NI) 2003; the same EH40 limits are conventionally applied there, but for a Northern Ireland-specific legal determination confirm with HSENI.

7. RE-VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (if this answer is to be relied on later)

1. Open hse.gov.uk/pubns/books/eh40.htm and confirm the edition currently posted.
2. Open Table 1 of that edition and read the carbon monoxide row by column, not by reading order.
3. Check the comment column for any date-limited qualifier.
4. Compare any candidate date-limited value's end date with the assessment date; if the end date is past, the general WEL applies to all sectors.
5. Cross-check ppm against mg.m-3 using the 1.1646 factor; a mismatch means a column has been misread.

# Approved Document B (Fire safety) Volume 1: Dwellings — sprinkler and common-stair trigger heights (England)

## 0. Answers at a glance

| Ask | Question | Answer | Status of the text relied on |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Governing document (constraint) | Approved Document B (Fire safety) Volume 1: Dwellings, 2019 edition incorporating the 2020 and 2022 amendments, **collated with the 2025, 2026 and 2029 amendments**, for use in England (GOV.UK consolidated PDF; Planning Portal: published July 2019, updated 2 March 2025) | Version identified, not a value ask — no numeric result |
| 2 | Top-storey height above ground above which blocks of flats should be fitted with a sprinkler system throughout | **11 m** — i.e. **more than 11 m** above ground level | In force (since 26 November 2020); unchanged by the 2022, 2025 and 2026 amendments |
| 3 | The same trigger height before the 2020 amendments | **30 m** — i.e. more than 30 m above ground level | Superseded text (2019 edition as published July 2019, and the 2006 edition as amended) |
| 4 | Top-storey height at which flats should be served by **more than one common stair** | **18 m** — ADB wording: a block of flats **with a storey 18 m or more in height** | In force (since 30 September 2026) |
| 5 | Date the changes introducing that multi-stair recommendation take effect | **30 September 2026**, for use in England | In force at the date of the source fetch (23 November 2026) |

All three figures are quoted directly from the published text; no interpolation has been done.

---

## 1. Version control (satisfying ask 1)

The answers are taken from the consolidated England text of **Approved Document B (Fire safety) Volume 1: Dwellings, 2019 edition incorporating the 2020 and 2022 amendments, collated with the 2025, 2026 and 2029 amendments** (GOV.UK asset `67d02309…`, SHA-256 prefix `b0b468a7`), cross-checked against:

- the 2019 edition **incorporating the 2020 amendments only** (asset `677fa136…`, `dde9a444`) — used for ask 3's before/after comparison;
- the 2019 edition **incorporating the 2020 and 2022 amendments** (asset `67d02386…`, `5ec1573c`) — used to confirm the 11 m figure survived the 2022 amendments;
- the **2026 amendments booklet** (asset `66d57a94…`, `852d8b8a`) — primary source for asks 4 and 5;
- the **May 2020 circular letter** (asset `924446…`, `d344799c`) — primary source for ask 3 and for the 2020 effective date.

Two scoping notes that matter for a defensible answer:

1. **The 2029 amendments are printed in the current PDF but are not in force.** They take effect **2 September 2029** for use in England. Ask 1's constraint expressly scopes the answer to "the 2020, 2022, 2025 and 2026 amendments", so the 2029 content is excluded. It should also be recorded that the 2026 booklet's own change log lists only two 2026 changes (multi-stair; evacuation-lift design provisions), and no fetched passage attributes any change to the 11 m sprinkler trigger or the 18 m stair trigger to the 2029 amendments.
2. **"Currently published" is date-sensitive.** At the source fetch date of 23 November 2026 the 2026 amendments (effective 30 September 2026) are in force, so answers 4 and 5 are live requirements of the current text, not future ones. Had the question been asked before 30 September 2026, ask 4 would have had no answer in ADB Vol 1 at all (single-stair design was the default), and ask 5 would have been a future date.

---

## 2. Ask 2 — Sprinkler trigger height in the current text: **more than 11 m**

**Source text (notes to Table B4, Minimum periods of fire resistance):**

> "2. Blocks of flats with a top storey more than 11m above ground level (see Diagram D6) should be fitted with a sprinkler system in accordance with Appendix E.
>
> NOTE: Sprinklers should be provided within the individual flats, they do not need to be provided in the common areas such as stairs, corridors or landings when these areas are fire sterile.
>
> 3. 'With sprinkler system' means that the building is fitted throughout with an automatic sprinkler system in accordance with Appendix E."

This wording is identical in the 2020-only, the 2020+2022 and the 2020+2022+2025+2026 collations — i.e. **the 11 m figure has not moved since 26 November 2020**, and the 2022, 2025 and 2026 amendments did not touch it.

**Engineering points a designer or building control body must apply to this answer:**

- **"Throughout" is defined, and is narrower than the plain English reading.** Note 3 defines "with sprinkler system" as fitted *throughout* in accordance with Appendix E, but the NOTE to note 2 records that sprinklers need be provided **within the individual flats** and not in common areas (stairs, corridors, landings) **where those areas are fire sterile**. "Fire sterile" means no fire load — a protected corridor used for resident storage, bin presentation or similar is not fire sterile, and the exemption does not then apply.
- **Standard.** Appendix E was not changed by the 2020 amendments; it recommends **BS 9251** for residential blocks of flats, or **BS EN 12845** for residential blocks of flats outside the scope of BS 9251.
- **Consequential effect on fire resistance.** The 2020 circular records that "Table B4 (Minimum periods of fire resistance) will also be amended when these changes take effect to reflect that a block of flats without a sprinkler system above 11 metres is not permitted if following the guidance in the Approved Document." A designer who departs from the 11 m sprinkler provision is therefore also departing from the Table B4 basis of the guidance and needs a fire-engineering justification covering fire resistance, not just the sprinkler omission.
- **Wording variance to be aware of.** The 2020 circular describes the trigger as "a top floor more than 11 metres above ground level" while ADB uses "top storey more than 11m". They are applied as the same trigger; ADB's "top storey" governs.
- **Boundary is exclusive.** "More than 11 m" — a block whose top storey is exactly 11.00 m does not trigger the note on a literal reading; 11.01 m does. Do not round down a design that lands on the boundary; resolve it with the building control body early.

---

## 3. Ask 3 — The trigger height before the 2020 amendments: **more than 30 m**

**Source text (May 2020 circular letter, 26 May 2020, "Summary of main changes"):**

> "**Sprinklers** — The amendments include a reduction in the height threshold for sprinklers in Purpose group 1a (residential (block of flats)) …"

and, in the "Main changes made by the 2020 amendments" page of the consolidated document:

> "a. **Sprinklers:** A reduction in the trigger height **from 30m to 11m**."

**Supporting corroboration that 30 m was the pre-2020 figure:** the same notes to Table B4 in the current text retain a 30 m trigger for non-residential uses — note 6: "Buildings within the 'office', 'shop and commercial', 'assembly and recreation', 'industrial' and 'storage and other non-residential' (except car parks for light vehicles) purpose groups (purpose groups 3 to 7(a)) require sprinklers where there is a top storey more than 30m above ground level." The 2020 amendment moved flats off the general 30 m figure and onto a dwelling-specific 11 m figure; the 30 m figure survives only for those non-residential purpose groups.

**Effective date of the change (for completeness, since ask 3 is a "before" value):** the 2020 amendments **take effect on 26 November 2020**, with transitional arrangements — they do not apply where a building notice or initial notice has been given, or full plans deposited, before that day and either the work started before 26 November 2020 or started before 29 January 2021. Blocks commenced under those arrangements legitimately remain on the 30 m basis.

**Do not confuse:** 30 m is no longer the flats trigger. Any answer that gives 30 m as the current figure for blocks of flats is reading the pre-2020 text or the purpose-group 3–7(a) note.

---

## 4. Ask 4 — More than one common stair: **a storey 18 m or more in height**

**Source text (2026 amendments booklet, "Summary of main changes" / "List of amendments"):**

> "The changes focus on the following fire safety provisions:
> a. **A new recommendation for more than one common stair to be provided in blocks of flats with a storey 18m or more in height.**
> b. Building design provisions to support the use of evacuation lifts in blocks of flats."

and in the consolidated Vol 1, "Changes made by the 2025, 2026 and 2029 amendments":

> "a. A new recommendation for more than one common stair to be provided in blocks of flats with a storey 18m or more in height."

**Where it lands in the document:** Section 3 (Means of escape – flats), subheading "Number of escape routes", where the booklet replaces paragraph 3.27 ("From the flat entrance door, a single escape route is acceptable in either of the following cases…") and adds the multi-stair provision alongside it. The booklet's extract does not show the paragraph number of the new multi-stair provision itself; cite it as **Section 3, "Number of escape routes"**, with the amendment booklet's summary page, until the paragraph number is read off the printed page.

**Engineering points:**

- **Wording differs from the sprinkler note.** The 2026 text says "**a storey** 18 m or more in height" — it does **not** say "top storey". For a block of flats the highest storey governs, so in practice it is the top storey that is measured, but do not quote it as "top storey more than 18 m"; the trigger is the presence of any storey at or above 18 m.
- **Boundary is inclusive**, unlike the sprinkler trigger. "18 m or more" means a building with a storey at exactly 18.00 m **does** attract the recommendation; a building with a storey at 17.9 m does not.
- **Interaction with ask 2.** Any block caught by the 18 m stair recommendation is necessarily more than 11 m, so from 30 September 2026 a block with a storey at 18 m or above attracts **both** the throughout-sprinkler provision (Table B4 note 2) **and** the two-common-stair recommendation. A worked boundary set:
  - top storey 10.5 m → no sprinklers, single stair acceptable;
  - top storey 11.0 m → literal reading: no sprinkler requirement; single stair acceptable;
  - top storey 12.0 m → sprinklers required; single stair acceptable (subject to paragraph 3.27 conditions and protected lobby/corridor provisions);
  - top storey 18.0 m → sprinklers required **and** more than one common stair recommended.
- **It is guidance, not a statutory requirement in terms.** Like all ADB provisions it is one way of satisfying the Building Regulations; the recommendation is the deemed-to-satisfy route. Departure needs an equivalent-standard justification accepted by the building control body.
- **Companion change.** The same 2026 amendments introduce building design provisions supporting evacuation lifts in blocks of flats; a two-stair layout and evacuation-lift design should be developed together.

---

## 5. Ask 5 — Effective date: **30 September 2026**

**Source text (2026 amendments booklet, introduction):**

> "The changes highlighted in this amendment booklet **take effect on 30 September 2026 for use in England**. The 2019 edition incorporating the 2020, 2022 and 2025 amendments will continue to apply …"

and in the consolidated Vol 1:

> "**2026 amendments** — The 2026 amendments take effect on **30 September 2026** for use in England. The 2019 edition incorporating the 2020, 2022 and 2025 amendments will continue to apply where a building notice or an initial notice has been given to, or a building control approval application with full plans made to, the relevant authority before 30 September 2026 and either the building work to which it relates:
> a. has started and is sufficiently progressed before that day; or
> b. is started and is sufficiently progressed within the period of 18 months beginning on that day."

**Transitional effect — this is the point most often got wrong:**

- The **implementation date is 30 September 2026**, not the booklet's publication date (the booklet records "First published March 2024; Updated September 2024; Taking effect on 30 September 2026"). A building control application made in 2024/2025 does not bring the multi-stair recommendation forward; it is the notice/deposit date plus progress test that decides.
- Where a building notice, initial notice or full-plans application was made **before 30 September 2026** and the work either **started and is sufficiently progressed before that day**, or **is started and sufficiently progressed within the 18 months beginning on that day (i.e. by 30 March 2028)**, the pre-2026 text (2019 edition incorporating the 2020, 2022 and 2025 amendments) continues to apply — single-stair design remains available on that route.
- The same structure applies to the 2025 amendments, which **take effect on 2 March 2025** for use in England (their listed changes — including new sprinkler provisions for care homes — do not alter the flats trigger in ask 2).

---

## 6. Threshold disambiguation table (all figures appearing in ADB Vol 1 that are commonly confused)

| Height | Provision | Wording / trigger | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **11 m** | **Sprinklers throughout, blocks of flats** | **more than 11 m** (exclusive) | Table B4 note 2 (2020 amendments) |
| 11 m | Wayfinding signage for the fire service | storeys over 11 m | 2020 amendments |
| 11 m | Secure information box | storeys over 11 m | 2022 amendments |
| 11 m | External wall / Section 10 provisions for residential (purpose groups 1 and 2) | storey 11 m or more | 2022 amendments |
| 18 m | Evacuation alert systems | storeys over 18 m | 2022 amendments |
| **18 m** | **More than one common stair, blocks of flats** | **a storey 18 m or more** (inclusive) | **2026 amendments, effective 30 September 2026** |
| 18 m | "Very large" dwellinghouses outside the scope of dwellinghouse guidance | more than 18 m (or 10 m deep basement) | Table B4 note 4 |
| 30 m | Sprinklers, purpose groups 3–7(a) (non-residential) | more than 30 m | Table B4 note 6 |
| **30 m** | **Pre-2020 sprinkler trigger for flats (superseded)** | **more than 30 m** | **2019 edition before the 2020 amendments** |

---

## 7. Verification trail and residual uncertainty

**Verified by direct quotation:** the 11 m sprinkler trigger (three separate collations, identical wording); the 30 m pre-2020 figure (2020 circular + change-log page, "from 30m to 11m"); the 18 m multi-stair figure (2026 booklet + consolidated change log, identical wording); the 30 September 2026 effective date (2026 booklet introduction + consolidated change log, identical wording). No figure in this answer contradicts a limit stated elsewhere in this answer: 18 m > 11 m, so the stated interaction (both provisions apply at ≥18 m) is consistent; the exclusive/inclusive distinction is stated explicitly wherever the boundary is discussed.

**Residual points a reviewer should close on the printed page (they do not change the four values, but they do change how they are cited):**

1. **Diagram D6 datum.** Table B4 note 2 refers to Diagram D6 for the measurement of "top storey … above ground level". The fetched extracts do not reproduce the diagram. The convention applied in practice is measurement from ground level to the **top of the floor of the top storey** of the topmost storey; confirm against Diagram D6 in the copy held before applying the answer to a design sitting on the boundary (11.0 m / 18.0 m).
2. **Paragraph number of the multi-stair provision.** The 2026 booklet replaces paragraph 3.27 and introduces the subheading "Number of escape routes"; the new provision's own paragraph number is not visible in the extract. Cite Section 3 plus the booklet until confirmed.
3. **2029 amendments.** Present in the current PDF but not in force until 2 September 2029 and outside ask 1's stated scope. If the question is re-run after that date, re-check whether any 2029 change touches the 11 m or 18 m triggers before reusing these answers.
4. **Wales/Scotland/Northern Ireland.** These answers are England-only, as ask 1 requires. The Welsh ADB Vol 1 and the Scottish Technical Handbooks have different triggers and must not be substituted.

---

## 8. One-line answers for issue to a design team

- Sprinklers throughout: blocks of flats with a **top storey more than 11 m** above ground level (Table B4 note 2; sprinklers within flats, common areas only where not fire sterile; BS 9251 / BS EN 12845 per Appendix E).
- Before the 2020 amendments that figure was **more than 30 m** (reduced to 11 m by the 2020 amendments, effective **26 November 2020**, with transitional relief for work commenced under the pre-2020 text).
- More than one common stair: blocks of flats **with a storey 18 m or more in height**, recommended by the 2026 amendments, **taking effect 30 September 2026** for use in England (transitional relief for applications made before that date and sufficiently progressed before it, or started and sufficiently progressed by 30 March 2028).
