# Class R (EMI/RF) Bond Requirement — NASA-STD-4003A, w/Change 1

## 1. Bottom line

**There is no maximum RF impedance in ohms at a stated frequency for a Class R bond in NASA-STD-4003A.** The standard does not contain one, at any frequency. The question as asked has a false premise, and any answer of the form "X ohms at Y MHz per NASA-STD-4003A" is not traceable to the standard.

What the standard *actually* requires for Class R is a **DC bond resistance of 2.5 milliohms (0.0025 Ω) or less across each bonding joint, with low inductance**, achieved preferentially by **direct metal-to-metal contact**, with **no jumpers** and a short, wide strap only as a last resort.

## 2. The Class R requirement, as written

Source: NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, Table 1, "Summary of Electrical Bonding Classes" (p. 15 of 47), and Appendix B.3.1, "Design Parameters." Retrieved from the NASA Technical Standards System (standards.nasa.gov), document revalidated 03/13/2026.

**Table 1, Class R column — verbatim:**

| Table 1 field | Class R entry |
|---|---|
| BOND REQMT. | "Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort." |
| DC BOND RESISTANCE REQMT. | "Bonding resistance requirement, 2.5 milliohms or less. Low inductance required." |
| FREQ. REQMT. | High |
| CURRENT REQMT. | Low |

**Appendix B.3.1 — verbatim, in the worked example of a box that needs both Class R and Class H:**

> "It would require Class R bonding for RF and Class H bonding for fault current protection. Since both classes are applicable, the bond should be low inductance with no more than 2.5 milliohms dc resistance for Class R, and the contact area should be adequate to carry the maximum fault current that could occur for Class H."

**Independent corroboration — MSFC-HDBK-3697 (Electrical Bonding Design Guide Handbook, Baseline, 24 Mar 2014), §4.3:**

> "Historically, the Class R bond has been associated with a 2.5 mohm resistance across each bonding joint. The resistance of a bond joint does not change with frequency. Unfortunately, there are no purely resistive joints in the real world. All circuits, including bonding paths, contain elements of capacitance and inductance that have reactances that vary with frequency."

That handbook sentence is the crux: the 4003A Class R number is a **DC resistance**, and it is frequency-invariant by definition. The standard compensates for the frequency dependence of a real joint not with an impedance number but with a **qualitative design mandate** — low inductance, direct contact, no jumpers, short wide strap as last resort. The "FREQ. REQMT. = High" entry in Table 1 is a classification of the bond's *purpose* (it must work at high frequency), not a numeric impedance at a stated frequency.

## 3. Why there is no "ohms at a stated frequency" figure

- The standard's compliance metric for Class R is a **4-wire DC resistance measurement**, not a network-analyzer impedance measurement. No test frequency, no test fixture, and no impedance magnitude limit are defined for Class R anywhere in 4003A.
- A DC resistance limit is deliberately used because it is a *producibility and workmanship* screen (surface finish, faying-surface contact area, fastener torque, corrosion control), while the RF performance is controlled by the **inductance** of the path — which is controlled by geometry (direct contact, short/wide strap, no pigtails), not by a resistance number.
- Consequently, if a program needs an actual RF impedance figure at a frequency, it does not come from 4003A. It comes from one of: (a) program-level tailoring of 4003A, (b) a derived requirement in the EMI/EMC control plan, (c) MIL-STD-464 (system-level), or (d) a transfer-impedance specification on a shield/connector. Do not cite 4003A for such a number.

## 4. Non-normative illustration (NOT a NASA-STD-4003A requirement)

To show a reviewer why the standard refuses to state a single-frequency number, take a joint that just meets the limit, R = 2.5 mΩ, with a typical short direct-contact inductance of L = 10 nH:

|Z| = sqrt(R² + (2πfL)²)

- f = 1 MHz: |Z| ≈ 63 mΩ
- f = 10 MHz: |Z| ≈ 0.63 Ω
- f = 100 MHz: |Z| ≈ 6.3 Ω

The DC-compliant joint is already 250× its DC resistance at 1 MHz and 2500× at 100 MHz. This is exactly why the Class R requirement is written as "low inductance, direct contact, no jumpers" — the geometry clause, not a number, is what delivers the RF performance. Treat these figures as engineering context only; they are not a compliance limit and must not be cited as one.

## 5. Verification procedure the designer should actually specify

For each Class R joint on the drawing/ATP:

1. **Method:** 4-wire (Kelvin) DC resistance measurement with a calibrated milliohmmeter. Do not use a 2-wire DMM; lead and probe resistance swamps a 2.5 mΩ limit.
2. **Limit:** ≤ 2.5 mΩ **across each bonding joint** — per joint, not end-to-end. A box-to-structure path through three joints is three joints at 2.5 mΩ each, not one 2.5 mΩ path. This is the single most common misapplication of the Class R number.
3. **Probe placement:** probe on bare, clean metal immediately either side of the joint interface; probe pressure and tip geometry fixed and recorded. Subtract probe/lead zero (short the tips on the same material).
4. **Condition:** measure in the as-built, as-finished configuration (after plating/coating and torque-up), and record surface finish and torque value on the record.
5. **Design compliance (checked by inspection, not by meter):** direct metal-to-metal contact present; no jumper used; if a strap is used, it is short and wide (low L/D ratio, flat braid or sheet, not round wire with long pigtails); fasteners torqued to drawing; faying surfaces are conductive finishes.
6. **Drawing note, suggested wording:** "THE RESISTANCE ACROSS THIS JOINT SHALL BE LESS THAN 2.5 MILLIOHMS TO MEET THE ELECTRICAL BOND REQUIREMENTS OF NASA-STD-4003, CLASS R. DIRECT METAL-TO-METAL CONTACT REQUIRED; NO JUMPERS." (This note form follows the MSFC-HDBK-3697 §6.2 example notes.)

## 6. Design guidance that actually drives Class R success

- **Finish:** bare/chem-film (MIL-DTL-5541 Type II or III, Class 3, conductive) aluminum faying surfaces; no anodize, no paint, no primer in the bond path. Mask bond areas before finishing.
- **Geometry:** maximize contact area and minimize loop length; the inductance, not the resistance, is what fails EMC tests.
- **Jumpers:** the standard says no jumpers for Class R. Where a jumper is unavoidable (assembly/serviceability), use flat braid, as short and wide as physically possible, bonded at both ends with the same 2.5 mΩ per-joint limit at each end — and treat it as a deviation with rationale.
- **Corrosion:** avoid dissimilar-metal couples (e.g., aluminum-to-CFRP, aluminum-to-stainless) without a compatible conductive interface; a joint that passes at build can exceed 2.5 mΩ after humidity/temperature cycling. Specify the resistance check after environmental exposure for critical bonds.
- **Multi-class joints:** if the joint is also Class H (fault current), the strictest requirement of each class applies simultaneously — 2.5 mΩ DC *and* low inductance for Class R, plus adequate contact area to carry the Class H fault current (per Appendix B.3.1).

## 7. Citation block for the design record

- NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, *Electrical Bonding for NASA Launch Vehicles, Spacecraft, Payloads, and Flight Equipment*, approved for public release, distribution unlimited; revalidated 03/13/2026.
  - Table 1, Summary of Electrical Bonding Classes, p. 15 of 47 — Class R row.
  - §4.1, Electrical Bonding ([EBR 5], multiple-purpose bonds).
  - Appendix B.3.1, Design Parameters — "no more than 2.5 milliohms dc resistance for Class R." (Appendix A.3.1 in the pre-Change-1 printing.)
- MSFC-HDBK-3697, *Electrical Bonding Design Guide Handbook*, Baseline, 24 Mar 2014, §4.3 (RF/Class R bonding) and §6.2 (drawing note examples).

## 8. What was and was not verified against the controlled document

Verified from retrieved primary text: the Class R row of Table 1, the FREQ./CURRENT classification entries, and the Appendix B.3.1 sentence stating 2.5 mΩ DC for Class R. Also verified: the document revision and revalidation date, and that NASA-STD-4003A supersedes the base NASA-STD-4003.

Not verified, and to be confirmed against the controlled copy before quoting in a CDR package: the exact **EBR paragraph number** in Section 4 that carries the Class R resistance requirement itself (the retrieved excerpts contained §4.1 and [EBR 5] but not the Class R-specific EBR line). The value (2.5 mΩ) is not in doubt — it is corroborated in two independent places in the standard and again in the MSFC handbook — but the paragraph citation should be filled in from the controlled copy rather than from memory.

## 9. Direct answer to the designer

You cannot get an "ohms at a frequency" number out of 4003A, because the standard does not define one. Design and verify to **2.5 mΩ DC per joint with a low-inductance, direct-contact geometry**, and if your program genuinely needs an RF impedance limit at a frequency, raise it as a program-tailored or derived requirement and state its source explicitly — do not attribute it to NASA-STD-4003A.

## Findings (NOAA CO-OPS, verbatim)

**Source of record:** NOAA CO-OPS, National Tidal Datum Epoch page — https://www.tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/ (fetched 2026-11-23T11:56:46Z, sha256 4fa508e48279…). Corroborating source: CO-OPS Tidal Analysis Datum Calculator — https://access.co-ops.nos.noaa.gov/datumcalc/ (fetched 2026-11-23T11:56:47Z, sha256 2999991682c4…). A third corroboration: CO-OPS ArcGIS `Datums_Stations` iteminfo (mapservices.weather.noaa.gov).

### Ask 1 — constraint: authority is NOAA CO-OPS
All three values below are taken from NOAA Center for Operational Oceanographic Products and Services (CO-OPS) pages on tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov and access.co-ops.nos.noaa.gov — the office that establishes and publishes U.S. tidal datums. No third-party summary, news article, or secondary source was used.

### Ask 2 — Current 19-year NTDE: **1983–2001**
NTDE page, verbatim:

> "NOAA currently utilizes the 1983-2001 National Tidal Datum Epoch. This epoch is now undergoing revision and will be replaced by the fifth iteration of the NTDE."

Corroboration — Datum Calculator epoch selector offers `Present (1983 - 2001)`; the CO-OPS `Datums_Stations` layer description states "The 'Present Epoch' is from 1983-2001 and includes the latest datums available."

### Ask 3 — Fifth (replacement) epoch water-level data years: **2002–2020**
NTDE page, verbatim:

> "Measurements for the update will be based on water level data spanning the years 2002-2020."

Corroboration — Datum Calculator offers a `New (2002 - 2020)` epoch, and its warning dialog reads: "You have requested to compute datums for your data relative to the 2002-2020 National Tidal Datum Epoch, which has not yet been released by NOAA."

### Ask 4 — Proposed release year for new-epoch products: **2029**
NTDE page, verbatim:

> "The current proposed release date for new NTDE products is in 2029."

Corroboration — Datum Calculator warning: preliminary control datums "may be different from those that are planned to be officially released in early 2029."

## Verification / internal consistency
- The NTDE is defined on the same page as "a 19-year time period established by the National Ocean Service for collecting observations on water levels and calculating tidal datum values."
- 1983–2001 inclusive = 2001 − 1983 + 1 = **19 years** ✓
- 2002–2020 inclusive = 2020 − 2002 + 1 = **19 years** ✓
- The fifth epoch begins the calendar year immediately after the present epoch closes (2001 → 2002): no gap, no overlap. ✓
- Both the prose page and the calculator independently give 2029, so the release year is not an artifact of a single stale page.

## Caveats a downstream user should carry
1. **2029 is a stated target, not a contractual commitment.** Both NOAA pages call it "proposed" / "planned"; it is subject to revision. Treat it as the currently published proposal, which is exactly what the question asks.
2. **The 2002–2020 epoch is not yet official.** NOAA's own calculator labels datums computed on it "Preliminary, unofficial… for planning purposes only." Official U.S. tidal datums (on nautical charts, tide tables, and datum pages) remain on 1983–2001 until the new epoch is released.
3. **Currency of the answer:** values are as published on the pages fetched 2026-11-23. NOAA CO-OPS pages can lag announcements; the two-source agreement above reduces, but does not eliminate, that risk. If a later check shows a revised release year, only Ask 4 changes — the epoch years (1983–2001 present; 2002–2020 replacement) are fixed by the observation record and are stable.

## Answer in one line
NOAA CO-OPS currently bases official U.S. tidal datums on the **1983–2001** National Tidal Datum Epoch; the replacement fifth epoch will use water-level data spanning **2002–2020**; NOAA currently proposes releasing products based on the new epoch in **2029**.

question: X38
shape: Traffic signals, FHWA MUTCD (11th Edition vs 2009)
answer:
TRAFFIC ENGINEERING ANSWER — MUTCD pedestrian interval timing (11th Ed., Dec. 2023, incl. Rev. 1) vs. 2009 MUTCD

1. ANSWERS

| # | Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Minimum buffer interval (steady UPRAISED HAND) after the pedestrian change interval, before release of a conflicting vehicular movement | 2 seconds (minimum; a floor, not a target) | MUTCD 11th Ed., §4I.06, ¶04 (Standard) |
| 2 | Default walking speed for sizing pedestrian clearance time | 3.5 ft/s (≈1.07 m/s), reduced where slower pedestrians or wheelchair users routinely use the crosswalk | MUTCD 11th Ed., §4I.06, ¶¶07–16 with ¶10 (Guidance) establishing 3.5 ft/s as the baseline |
| 3 | Buffer-interval minimum in the 2009 MUTCD | 3 seconds | MUTCD 2009, §4E.06, ¶3 (Standard) — same requirement, older section numbering |

Net change 2009 → 11th Ed.: the buffer minimum was reduced from 3 s to 2 s, while simultaneously being made unconditional (the buffer must now always be provided and displayed, not merely before a conflicting release).

2. GOVERNING TEXT — 11th EDITION, §4I.06 (verbatim, Standard ¶04)

"A pedestrian change interval consisting of a flashing UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall begin immediately following the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) signal indication. Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement. The sum of the time of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval shall not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time (see Paragraphs 7 through 16 of this Section). The buffer interval shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used."

Three binding constraints are packed into that paragraph and all three must be satisfied simultaneously by any timing plan:
(a) buffer ≥ 2.0 s, ending no earlier than the instant the conflicting vehicular movement is released;
(b) (pedestrian change interval) + (buffer) ≥ calculated pedestrian clearance time (PCT);
(c) buffer start ≤ start of red clearance interval, if a red clearance interval is used.

Figure 4I-4 note (11th Ed.) reinforces that the buffer is not optional: "The Buffer Interval, which shall always be provided and displayed, may be used to help satisfy the calculated pedestrian clearance time, or may begin after the calculated pedestrian clearance time has ended." The same figure shows the permitted relationships to the concurrent vehicular phase: Yellow Change Interval = Buffer Interval, or Yellow Change Interval + Red Clearance Interval = Buffer Interval. In ordinary operation the 2 s floor is therefore usually exceeded incidentally, because the buffer typically spans a 3 s or longer yellow plus red clearance.

3. WALKING SPEED — WHAT "DEFAULT" MEANS

The 11th Edition fixes 3.5 ft/s as the speed the pedestrian clearance time is sized for unless a documented reason exists to go slower. §4I.06 ¶10 (Guidance) reads verbatim:

"Where pedestrians who walk slower than 3.5 feet per second, or pedestrians who use wheelchairs, routinely use the crosswalk, a walking speed of less than 3.5 feet per second should be considered in determining the pedestrian clearance time."

Engineering reading: 3.5 ft/s is the default/nominal design speed; it is a ceiling on the design speed, not a floor. The adjustment is one-directional — you may and often should go slower (common practice: 3.0 ft/s at schools, senior centers, hospitals, transit stations, APS-equipped crossings in such areas), never faster. 3.5 ft/s is unchanged from the 2009 MUTCD, so this is not a source of discrepancy between editions.

4. 2009 MUTCD COMPARISON (ask 3)

MUTCD 2009, §4E.06 "Pedestrian Intervals and Signal Phases," ¶3 (Standard), contained the parallel provision:

"Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 3 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement."

Context that matters for a reviewer: the buffer interval as a named requirement was introduced by the 2009 MUTCD (the 2003 MUTCD had no buffer-interval requirement; it relied on the pedestrian change interval plus the vehicular change/clearance intervals). The 11th Edition retained the mechanism, lowered the numeric floor to 2 s, and strengthened the obligation to display the buffer in every pedestrian phase.

Note on evidence: the 2009 quotation above is reproduced from the published 2009 MUTCD text from professional knowledge — the fetched source set for this task did not include the 2009 edition. It is a one-lookup verification: 2009 MUTCD PDF (mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/pdfs/2009r1r2/), Part 4, Chapter 4E, §4E.06, ¶3. The 11th Edition values (2 s; 3.5 ft/s) are directly supported by the fetched primary text.

5. HOW TO APPLY IT — CONTROLLER TIMING PROCEDURE

Step 1. Compute PCT = crossing distance (ft, curb to far curb or to a refuge median of adequate width) ÷ walking speed (ft/s). Use 3.5 ft/s by default; use a lower value where warranted per ¶10, and document the justification in the timing sheet.
Step 2. Assign the walk interval: 7 s guidance minimum, 4 s permitted option where pedestrian volumes/characteristics allow (§4I.06 ¶¶11–12).
Step 3. Set buffer = 2 s minimum. Set pedestrian change interval (flashing DONT WALK) ≥ PCT − buffer.
Step 4. Verify constraint (a): the conflicting vehicular movement's green must not start until the buffer has been displayed for ≥ 2 s. Verify (b): flashing + buffer ≥ PCT. Verify (c): buffer start ≤ red clearance start.
Step 5. Round upward to the controller's whole-second resolution; never round a minimum down.

Worked example (check arithmetic against the constraints above):
• Crosswalk length 60 ft, default speed 3.5 ft/s → PCT = 60 ÷ 3.5 = 17.14 s.
• Buffer = 2.0 s (minimum).
• Flashing DONT WALK ≥ 17.14 − 2.0 = 15.14 s → program 15.2 s (or 16 s at whole-second resolution).
• Check (b): 15.2 + 2.0 = 17.2 s ≥ 17.14 s ✓. Check (a): buffer 2.0 s ≥ 2.0 s ✓.
• Total pedestrian phase = walk 7.0 + flashing 15.2 + buffer 2.0 = 24.2 s; the concurrent through movement's yellow + red clearance must be long enough that the buffer does not delay the release beyond the intended coordination offset — if it does, lengthen the flashing interval, not shorten the buffer.

6. QA / REVIEW CHECKLIST

• Is the buffer ≥ 2 s and does it terminate at or before the conflicting green? (11th Ed. floor)
• Is flashing + buffer ≥ PCT computed at 3.5 ft/s or a documented slower speed?
• Is a slower speed used where the crossing serves a hospital, school, senior housing, transit stop, or APS-equipped crossing with high older-adult/wheelchair use? If not, is the omission justified in writing?
• Does the buffer start no later than the red clearance start?
• Are legacy 3 s buffers being retained? That is compliant — 3 s ≥ 2 s. There is no need to retime to shorten a 3 s buffer, and doing so would consume the safety margin the 2009 standard provided.
• If a local/state supplement is in force, check it: several state supplements restate §4I.06 with the same 2 s floor (e.g., the Ohio supplement to the 11th Ed. reproduces ¶04 with 'at least 2 seconds'), but supplements can be more restrictive and govern where they are.

7. SCOPE AND ASSUMPTIONS

• Edition: 11th Edition, December 2023, with Revision 1 (December 2025) incorporated. The fetched Revision 1 sources reproduce §4I.06 ¶04 with the 2 s minimum, so the Revision 1 text does not change the answer.
• Scope is standard signalized/midblock pedestrian crossings. Exclusive pedestrian phases, leading pedestrian intervals, PHBs (Part 4J), and APS timing adjustments do not alter the 2 s buffer floor or the 3.5 ft/s default; they add requirements on top of them.
• Countdown-related guidance (§4I.04 ¶07) — flashing set to approximately 4 s less than the required PCT with an additional steady-DONT-WALK clearance interval where there is no concurrent vehicular phase — is a separate provision and does not modify the 2 s minimum in §4I.06.
• Out of my function as Traffic Engineer: this answer does not opine on legal liability, on whether a jurisdiction must retroactively retime existing signals (the MUTCD minimum is a floor; existing 3 s buffers already comply), or on the FHWA rulemaking rationale beyond noting the numeric change.

question: X39
shape: Oil spill prevention, US EPA (SPCC applicability)
answer:
# SPCC Applicability — Two Capacity Ceilings and the Aboveground Counting Rule

Scope: a U.S. onshore industrial facility that is non-transportation-related (not a vessel, not a pipeline) and stores oil in aboveground drums and tanks plus some completely buried tanks. The question is regulatory-text applicability, not a facility inventory; no container capacities were supplied, so the deliverable is the rule plus a counting procedure a engineer can apply directly.

## 1. The two cealings (ask 1, 2, 3)

| # | Storage category | Ceiling — must stay AT OR UNDER | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Aggregated aboveground storage capacity | **1,320 U.S. gallons of oil** | 40 CFR 112.1(f)(2)(ii) |
| 2 | Completely buried storage capacity | **42,000 U.S. gallons of oil** | 40 CFR 112.1(f)(2)(i) |

Both must hold. 112.1(f)(2) exempts a facility only if it 'meets both of the following requirements' — (i) buried ≤42,000 and (ii) aboveground ≤1,320. Exceeding either one alone puts the facility inside Part 112, irrespective of the other.

Boundary semantics (ask 3). The rule's own words are '…or less', and EPA's applicability flowchart asks whether the total is 'greater than 1,320' / 'greater than 42,000'. Therefore exactly 1,320 gal and exactly 42,000 gal are OUTSIDE coverage; 1,321 and 42,001 are inside. Two practical consequences: (i) the comparison is against capacity, not against oil on hand, so a drum that is empty but not permanently closed still counts; (ii) a facility sitting exactly at a cealing has zero headroom — one additional 55-gal drum takes it inside — so operate with margin and re-run the calculation on any change.

Beating both cealings is necessary but not sufficient for non-coverage. The other applicability tests still apply: the facility must be non-transportation-related, must be engaged in drilling, producing, gathering, storing, processing, refinning, transferring, distributing, using, or consuming oil, and must not be able to reasonably be expected to discharge oil in quantities that may be harmful into navigable waters or adjoining shorelines. If those are met and either cealing is exceeded, a SPCC Plan is required under 112.3.

## 2. Which aboveground containers count toward the 1,320 (ask 4)

A container is counted toward the aboveground total when ALL of the following hold:

1. **It is an aboveground container, or is treated as one.** The container-inclusion list in 112.1 (the paragraph immediately preceding (c); cited in secondary references as 112.1(b)) provides that any 'bunkered tank' or 'partially buried tank' as defined in 112.2, or any container in a vault, is each considered an aboveground storage container for purposes of Part 112. Completely buried tanks are NOT in this total (they go to the 42,000 side).
2. **Its storage capacity is 55 U.S. gallons or greater.** 112.1(f)(2)(ii): 'only containers with a capacity of 55 U.S. gallons or greater are counted'; 112.1(f)(5) separately exempts 'any container with a storage capacity of less than 55 gallons of oil'. 55 gal exactly counts; 54.9 gal does not.
3. **It is counted at full nameplate capacity**, regardless of how full it is. The inclusion list expressly covers any container 'used for standby storage, for seasonal storage, or for temporary storage, or not otherwise permanently closed' — so idle, empty, or half-full drums and tanks count unless they meet the 112.2 definition of 'permanently closed'.
4. **It is not on the exclusion list** below.

### Excluded from the aboveground total
Per 112.1(f)(2)(ii)(A)-(F) and the parallel exemptions in 112.1(f)(5)-(12):

- **(A)** The capacity of a container that is 'permanently closed' as defined in 112.2 (emptied of oil, vented, and rendered inoperable by removing and capping all connecting pipes — and recorded/marked as such). An empty drum that has NOT been rendered permanently closed still counts.
- **(B)/(7)** Motive power containers as defined in 112.2 — containers that supply fuel to an engine that propels a motor vehicle, motor vehicle, or vessel (vehicle fuel tanks, locomotive/aircraft tanks). Caveat: 112.1(f)(7) states that the transfer of fuel or other oil into a motive power container at an otherwise regulated facility does not inherit this exclusion.
- **(C)/(8)** Hot-mix asphalt, or any hot-mix asphalt container.
- **(D)/(9)** Any container for heating oil used solely at a single-family residence.
- **(E)/(10)** Pesticide application equipment and related mix containers.
- **(F)/(12)** Any milk and milk product container and associated piping and appurtenances.
- **Containers under 55 gal** (112.1(f)(5)).
- **Storage containers used exclusively for wastewater treatment.** EPA's applicability guidance instructs 'Do not include … storage containers used exclusively for wastewater treatment'; the reguly structure rests on 112.1(f)(6) (any facility or part thereof used exclusively for wastewater treatment and not used to satisfy any requirement of Part 112), with the caveat that 'the production, recovery, or recycling of oil is not wastewater treatment'.
- **(Not containers, but commonly miscounted)** Intra-facility gathering lines subject to 49 CFR 192 or 195 (112.1(f)(11)) — piping volume is not part of any container total.

### Drums specifically
A 55-gal drum counts in full (55 gal); a 30-gal drum, 5-gal pail, or 1-gal can does not. Intermediate bulk containers (e.g., 275-gal IBCs/totes) count in full. Twenty-four 55-gal drums alone equal 1,320 gal — i.e., a drum farm can reach the cealing with no tank at all.

## 3. Which buried tanks count toward the 42,000

**Counted:** 'completely buried tanks' as defined in 112.2 — tanks that are completely buried and are not aboveground, bunkered, or partially buried (those three go to the aboveground side).

**Excluded** from the completely buried storage capacity (112.1(f)(2)(i); EPA's applicability page states the same list):
- Completely buried tanks subject to ALL of the technical requirements of 40 CFR 280 or 281. Note 'all' — a tank deferred from, or excluded from, any 280 technical requirement does not qualify for this exclusion and its capacity counts.
- Containers with a storage capacity of less than 55 gal.
- Permanently closed containers.
- Containers used exclusively for wastewater treatment.

**Bburied piping is not counted:** the category is 'completely buried tank', not piping; buried piping volume does not enter the 42,000 sum (though it is a potential discharge source and belongs in the facility diagram if the facility is regulated).

## 4. Procedure to apply at the facility

1. **Define the facility boundary.** Aggregate every container under common ownership at the contiguous site; do not split a site into convenient sub-areas to stay under a cealing.
2. **Inventory every container** that holds or is intended to hold oil: nameplate capacity (gal), location class (aboveground / bunkered / partially buried / in a vault / completely buried), status (in service, standby, seasonal, temporary, permanently closed), and exclusion basis if any.
3. **Compute A** = Σ capacity of aboveground-class containers with capacity ≥55 gal, less the exclusions in §2.
4. **Compute B** = Σ capacity of completely buried tanks with capacity ≥55 gal, less 280/281-regulated tanks and the other exclusions in §3.
5. **Compare:** outside coverage on capacity grounds if **A ≤ 1,320 AND B ≤ 42,000**; inside if **A > 1,320 OR B > 42,000**. Then confirm the non-transportation / oil-handling / reasonable-potential-to-discharge tests.
6. **Document** the container list, the arithmetic, and the definitional basis for each exclusion — this is the audit trail, and it becomes the basis of the facility diagram and Plan if the facility is regulated.
7. **Re-run** whenever a container is added, replaced, returned to service, or reclassified (e.g., a 'permanently closed' drum put back in service).

### Worked illustration (hypothetical — arithmetic demonstration only; no facility data were supplied)
- 12 × 55-gal drums (660) + 1,000-gal aboveground tank (1,000) + 500-gal partially buried tank (500, counted as aboveground) → A = 2,160 gal > 1,320 → **inside** Part 112 on the aboveground test alone, whatever B is.
- Remove the partially buried tank and reduce to 6 drums → 330 + 1,000 = 1,330 > 1,320 → still **inside**.
- Reduce to 5 drums → 275 + 1,000 = 1,275 ≤ 1,320 → **outside** on the aboveground test, provided B ≤ 42,000 gal and the other applicability tests are not met.

## 5. What this determination does NOT decide (avoid misapplying the numbers)

- **Substantial-harm / Facility Response Plan.** Appendix F uses different figures and different tests — 'total oil storage capacity ≥42,000 gallons' where operations include over-water transfers of oil to or from vessels, and '≥1 million gallons' with inadequate secondary containment. The 42,000 figure appears there in a different role; it is not a second applicability cealing.
- **Qualified Facility status.** The 10,000-gal total-capacity line in 112.6 governs self-certification of a Plan, not whether a Plan is needed.
- **Other programs.** State and local oil-storage rules, CWA §311(j) authority, the UST rules (40 CFR 280/281), and state-administered SPCC programs can apply below these cealings. The federal SPCC applicability cealings are a floor, not a safe harbor.
- **Unresolved by the quoted text — decide conservatively and document:** (i) oil-filled operational equipment (transformeres, hydralic power units, machining coolent reservoirs) — whether these are 'containers' at all; (ii) fuel tanks mounted on vehicles or trailers used exclusively on site (motive-power exclusion vs. counting); (iii) multiple non-contiguous parcels under one owner (one facility or several).

## 6. Citation note

Ceilings and exclusions are quoted from 40 CFR 112.1 as currently published (eCFR, fetched 2026-11-23) and from the CFR-2024 title 40 vol 24 PDF of 112.1; the boundary and the buried-side exclusion list are confirmed against EPA's applicability page ('Does the SPCC Rule Apply to Your Facility?', fetched 2026-11-23). The eCFR snippet for 112.1(f)(2)(i) was truncated mid-sentence in the fetch, so the buried exclusions are stated here on EPA-applicability-page authority plus the parallel structure of (f)(2)(ii) — verify against the full regulatory text before relying on the 280/281 exclusion in a specific case.

shape: Units and conversions, HVAC capacity (NIST SP 811 conversion factors)
answer:
CHILLER CAPACITY CONVERSION — 10 TON (US) OF REFRIGERATION TO kW

ANSWER
  10 tons of refrigeration = 35.17 kW (four significant figures).
  Unrounded: 35.168 53 kW.

1. CONVERSION FACTOR USED (NIST, official)

Source: NIST Special Publication 811, Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI), Appendix B.9, table "Heat Flow Rate". Entry, quoted as published:

    ton of refrigeration (12 000 Btu_IT/h)  →  watt (W)  →  3.516 853 E+03

Therefore, exactly as NIST publishes it:

    1 ton of refrigeration = 3 516.853 W = 3.516 853 kW

This is the definitional entry NIST gives for the ton of refrigeration, keyed explicitly to the International Table Btu (Btu_IT) at 12 000 Btu_IT/h. No secondary or rounded source (e.g. the commonly quoted 3.517 kW/ton) is used.

2. INDEPENDENT CROSS-CHECK OF THE FACTOR FROM NIST'S OWN Btu_IT/h ENTRY

Same SP 811 Appendix B.9 table (Heat Flow Rate):

## 0. Bottom line

**Ask 2 — junction-to-ambient thermal resistance: NOT SPECIFIED in this datasheet.** DS40002061B contains no thermal-resistance data of any kind for the ATmega328P — no theta-JA, no theta-JC, no psi-JT, no thermal-resistance-vs-airflow table, no derating curve, no 'Thermal Considerations' section — for the 28-lead PDIP (package code 28P3) or for any of the other three packages in the family (32A TQFP, 28M1 QFN, 32M1-A QFN). The only thermal and current limits it does state are given in §1 below. The -55 degC to +125 degC figure in the Absolute Maximum Ratings is an operating (ambient) temperature range for the part, not a junction-temperature rating; the datasheet never uses 'junction temperature' as a limiting parameter.

Anyone quoting e.g. '45 degC/W' or '1 W at 25 degC' as an ATmega328P datasheet value is quoting a different document — a Microchip package thermal-data table, a JEDEC JESD51 report, a distributor page, or another AVR family (e.g. ATmega8/ATmega16-era datasheets, which did carry power-dissipation rows).

## 1. What DS40002061B actually specifies (the limits that do exist)

**§29.1 Absolute Maximum Ratings (ATmega328P electrical characteristics chapter, p. 308 in the 09/2020 printing — section number is stable, page numbers can shift by a page between printings):**

- Operating temperature: -55 degC to +125 degC
- Storage temperature: -65 degC to +150 degC
- Voltage on any pin except RESET with respect to ground: -0.5 V to VCC + 0.5 V
- Voltage on RESET with respect to ground: -0.5 V to +13.0 V
- Maximum operating voltage: 6.0 V
- DC current, VCC and GND pins: 200.0 mA
- DC current, any I/O pin: 40.0 mA
- DC current, RESET pin: 40.0 mA
- DC current, AVCC pin: 40.0 mA

Note the absence of any row containing the words 'thermal', 'junction', 'dissipation' or a theta symbol. The section carries the usual stress caveat that exposure to absolute-maximum conditions for extended periods may affect reliability.

**§29.2 DC Characteristics:** guaranteed over TA = -40 degC to +85 degC (industrial). The ordering table (p. 627) additionally lists -AN/-ANR and -PN/-PNR ordering codes specified over -40 degC to +105 degC.

**§29.3 Speed Grades:** 0-4 MHz @ 1.8-5.5 V, 0-10 MHz @ 2.7-5.5 V, 0-20 MHz @ 4.5-5.5 V.

**Ordering/package identification (p. 627):** ATmega328P-PU / -PN = package code 28P3 = '28-lead, 0.300 in Wide, Plastic Dual Inline Package (PDIP)'.

| Ask | Question | Ruling | Basis in DS40002061B |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | theta-JA of ATmega328P, 28-pin PDIP, degC/W | Not specified — no such parameter in the document | §29.1 and the whole electrical-characteristics chapter contain no thermal-resistance data; §39 (Packaging Information, 32A / 28M1 / 32M1-A / 28P3 drawings) is mechanical only |

## 3. If a theta-JA number is genuinely required — procedure

1. **Ask Microchip for it against the package code.** The correct request is for the thermal characteristics of package code 28P3 (28-lead, 0.300 in PDIP), not for the ATmega328P specifically — thermal resistance is a package property, so the same value applies to every device in a 28P3. Microchip publishes package thermal data separately from device datasheets (packaging specification pages and support-issued thermal data). Cite the package code in the request; a device-name request usually returns the datasheet you already have.
2. **If Microchip cannot supply it, measure or model it.** The governing standards are JEDEC JESD51-2 (still air), JESD51-3 (low-effective-thermal-conductivity test board) and JESD51-7 (high-effective-thermal-conductivity test board). A theta-JA quoted without its board and airflow condition is not usable for a design decision.
3. **If neither is available, use a labelled industry-typical value with margin.** For a 28-lead, 0.300 in PDIP in still air: theta-JA is typically in the 45-60 degC/W range on a JEDEC 2-layer board, falling toward 35-45 degC/W with a 4-layer board and copper spreading at the leads; theta-JC is typically 15-20 degC/W. **These are INDUSTRY-TYPICAL figures for the package family, not ATmega328P datasheet values.** Use the worst case (60 degC/W) and carry the label into any document you produce.
4. **Treat the result as a sanity check, not a qualification.** For this device the thermal path is the package leads only — a PDIP has no thermal pad and no exposed die pad. A socket adds contact resistance and a small thermal penalty; long unsupported leads in a socketed assembly are the dominant variability.

## 4. Worked thermal budget (DERIVED — not datasheet values)

Model: TJ = TA + theta-JA x P_D, with TJ held at the §29.1 absolute-maximum operating temperature of 125 degC purely as a stress ceiling (not a design target), and P_D capped by the §29.1 current limit of 200 mA through VCC/GND at 5.5 V = **1.10 W**.

| Assumed theta-JA (degC/W) | P_D ceiling at TA = 25 degC | P_D ceiling at TA = 85 degC | P_D ceiling at TA = 105 degC |
|---|---|---|---|
| 45 | 1.10 W (current limit binds; thermal would allow 2.22 W) | 0.89 W | 0.44 W |
| 50 | 1.10 W (current limit binds; thermal would allow 2.00 W) | 0.80 W | 0.40 W |
| 60 | 1.10 W (current limit binds; thermal would allow 1.67 W) | 0.67 W | 0.33 W |

Reading of the table: at room ambient the 200 mA current ceiling binds before the thermal ceiling; at high ambient the thermal budget binds first. Both ceilings are derived, neither is a datasheet rating.

**Reality check against actual device dissipation.** A normally operating ATmega328P at full clock and 5.5 V draws well under 20 mA (see the Icc rows in §29.2), i.e. under 110 mW; at 50 degC/W that is a junction rise of about 5.5 degC. **On-die temperature sensing (for trend only).** The ATmega328P has an internal temperature sensor on ADC8 (MUX = 1000b, §24.9 'Temperature Measurement'). Its absolute accuracy is about plus/minus 10 degC and it is uncalibrated, so it is usable for relative trending and for detecting self-heating, not for verifying an absolute TJ. Do not use it to close a thermal budget.
